findings.topic: Quantitative modelling of F1 tyre degradation and fuel-corrected lap pace for a 2022-2024 ground-effect-era race strategy simulator

key_findings.claim: Standard lap-time functional form: base lap time + fuel mass effect + tyre-age degradation, with degradation as linear / quadratic / cubic / logarithmic in tyre age. This is the canonical Heilmeier/TUM structure used across the field.
key_findings.detail: The TUM race-simulation (Heilmeier et al.) builds each lap as: t_lap = (t_q + t_gap_racepace)  [base race pace]  + t_car  [car/driver delta]  + m_fuel * t_lap_sens_mass  [fuel effect]  + t_tire(age)  [tyre degradation]  + situational terms (DRS, grid, start, traffic, pit). The tyre term has four selectable closed forms (verbatim from calc_tire_degradation.py): linear t_tire = k_0 + k_1_lin*age ; quadratic t_tire = k_0 + k_1_quad*age + k_2_quad*age^2 ; cubic t_tire = k_0 + k_1_cub*age + k_2_cub*age^2 + k_3_cub*age^3 ; logarithmic t_tire = k_0 + k_1_ln*ln(k_2_ln*age + 1). k_0 is the fresh-tyre time offset of the compound (the compound pace delta), and 'age' is tyre age in laps. The state-space paper (arXiv 2512.00640) writes the observation eq as y_t = alpha_t + gamma*fuel_t + eps_t, with alpha_t the latent tyre pace following alpha_{t+1} = alpha_t + nu (degradation drift), reset at pit stops.
key_findings.numbers: linear: t_tire=k_0+k_1_lin*age (s); quad adds k_2_quad*age^2 (s/lap^2); log: k_0+k_1_ln*ln(k_2_ln*age+1)

key_findings.claim: Fuel effect is modelled as linear in fuel mass: lap time penalty = fuel_mass_kg * mass_sensitivity, with the sensitivity ~0.03 s/kg (~0.3 s per 10 kg).
key_findings.detail: TUM uses t_fuel = m_fuel * t_lap_sens_mass (combustioncar.py: 'return Car.t_add_car(self) + self.m_fuel * t_lap_sens_mass'). t_lap_sens_mass is track-specific: 0.036 s/kg at Yas Marina 2017, 0.034 at Yas Marina 2019, and only 0.019 at Spielberg (short, low-fuel-sensitivity track). Starting fuel mass m_fuel is set to 110 kg (2019 races) / 105 kg (2017), and fuel burn b_fuel_perlap is 1.549-2.0 kg/lap (1.909 in 2017, 1.549 and 2.0 in two 2019 configs). Independent practitioner analysis (f1pace.com 2024) and a Prost-team example both use ~0.03 s/kg, ~100-110 kg start. Note F1 fuel-flow regs cap usable race fuel near 100-110 kg; max tank 110 kg.
key_findings.numbers: 0.03 s/kg typical (~0.3 s/10kg); range 0.019-0.036 s/kg track-dependent; start fuel 105-110 kg; burn 1.55-2.0 kg/lap

key_findings.claim: Compound pace offset (soft vs medium vs hard) is captured by k_0 (fresh-tyre offset) and differing degradation slopes. Real-world weekend deltas are roughly 0.5-1.0 s/lap per step in the ground-effect era, well below the FIA's original 1.2 s (M-H) and 2.2 s (S-H) targets.
key_findings.detail: In the state-space paper the per-compound fresh-tyre pace resets were centred at 69.5 s (hard), 69.0 s (medium), 68.5 s (soft) for the 2025 Austrian GP -> i.e. ~0.5 s/lap between adjacent compounds at that track. FIA's tender target was hard=baseline, medium ~1.2 s/lap faster, soft ~2.2 s/lap faster; but in practice (2023) Pirelli ran them much closer: medium ~0.5 s faster than hard, soft ~1.0 s faster than hard. FIA degradation target: ~2 s total performance drop reached by 22% of race distance (hard), 18% (medium), 10% (soft).
key_findings.numbers: k_0 / fresh offsets ~0.5 s/lap per compound step (Austria 2025); FIA target S-H 2.2s, M-H 1.2s; real 2023 ~1.0s (S-H), ~0.5s (M-H)

key_findings.claim: Typical tyre degradation slopes are roughly 0.02-0.06 s/lap/lap for well-managed stints, rising steeply (0.1-0.2 s/lap/lap) near the cliff or for soft compounds. The TUM linear coefficients k_1_lin sit in this range.
key_findings.detail: From TUM Yas Marina 2019 tireset_pars (linear model), per-driver k_1_lin: e.g. HAM ~0.051-0.052 s/lap (compounds A4/A6) but 0.1855 s/lap on the softest A7; RIC ~0.026-0.040 s/lap, 0.0575 on A7; MAG 0.01-0.079 s/lap. The Bayesian state-space study estimated Hamilton's degradation at 0.054 s/lap (hard) and 0.060 s/lap (medium) at the 2025 Austrian GP (95% CIs ~+/-0.004-0.009), with compound differences NOT statistically distinct. Real 2024 Bahrain-test wear ranged 0.1-0.2 s/lap. A healthy hard stint loses ~0.05 s/lap; a struggling stint 0.15+ s/lap.
key_findings.numbers: k_1_lin (TUM) 0.026-0.079 s/lap normal, up to 0.186 s/lap softest; state-space nu=0.054 s/lap hard, 0.060 s/lap medium; real 0.05-0.20 s/lap

key_findings.claim: The 'cliff' (sharp nonlinear pace drop) and warm-up are NOT captured by a pure linear model; TUM recommends the logarithmic form for warm-up-then-degrade shape, and adds an explicit cold-tyre penalty plus reduced-degradation multipliers for SC/VSC laps.
key_findings.detail: TUM applies t_add_coldtires = 1.0 s on the out-lap (age_curstint==0) for cold/un-warmed tyres. Tyre degradation under safety-car / FCY laps is scaled by mult_tiredeg_sc=0.25 and mult_tiredeg_fcy=0.5 (degradation 'ages' the tyre only fractionally). Heilmeier notes a tyre initially underperforms below optimal core temperature, peaks, then degrades -> the logarithmic model fits this best when data is rich; linear is the fallback for sparse data. The state-space time-varying extension explicitly captured a warm-up phase: degradation rate nu starts NEGATIVE (lap times improving as tyre warms, e.g. laps 28-38 of a stint) before turning positive. The cliff is best represented by quadratic/cubic forms or a separate threshold; pure linear cannot.
key_findings.numbers: cold-tyre penalty 1.0 s on out-lap; SC deg multiplier 0.25, FCY 0.5; warm-up = negative early nu

key_findings.claim: Graining and thermal degradation are physical mechanisms (not separate model terms in TUM) that show up as steeper/earlier degradation slopes; the 2022 ground-effect regs increased load sensitivity and overheating tendency.
key_findings.detail: Graining = localized rubber shearing from sliding (forms grains, reduces grip), worst when tyres are too cold / overworked; thermal degradation = carcass/compound overheating beyond optimal window, permanently hardening the rubber. The 2022 ground-effect cars are heavier with higher sustained loads and less low-speed downforce, aggravating graining; Pirelli's 18-inch construction was designed to reduce overheating. These manifest in a strategy model as compound-/track-specific increases in k_1 (slope) and onset of the cliff, or a temperature-window term; no standard closed-form constant exists, so they are typically fit per-event from FP long-run data.
key_findings.numbers: qualitative; modelled via elevated k_1 slopes / earlier cliff; no universal constant

key_findings.claim: Heilmeier et al. (TUM, 2018 'A Race Simulation for Strategy Decisions in Circuit Motorsports') models the race lap-wise (discrete per lap), summing base pace, fuel-mass loss, tyre degradation, pit losses and overtaking; tyre deg uses linear or logarithmic age functions, fuel uses a linear mass-sensitivity term.
key_findings.detail: Architecture: lap-discretized; each driver's lap = base lap time minus/plus deltas. Pit-stop modelling separates standstill (t_pit_tirechange_min ~1.9 s + team add ~0.4-1.4 s) from drive-through pit loss (t_pitdrive_inlap + t_pitdrive_outlap; e.g. Yas Marina outlap ~18 s, Spielberg ~11.4 s). The follow-up Monte-Carlo paper (Heilmeier 2020) adds probabilistic effects (random lap-time sigma via random.gauss, SC/FCY phases, accidents). Heilmeier 2020a found the logarithmic tyre model fit better than linear when data quality is high. The newer Bayesian state-space approach (arXiv 2512.00640, 2025) reframes the same lap-time = latent_tyre_pace + gamma*fuel + noise with a skewed-t error to handle driver-mistake outliers, beating an ARIMA(2,1,2) baseline (RMSPE 1.08 vs 1.52).
key_findings.numbers: pit standstill ~1.9s + 0.4-1.4s; pit drive-through ~11-18s; fuel coeff gamma (state-space) ~ matches 0.03 s/kg; SC base lap multiplier 1.6, FCY 1.4

concrete_numbers: Lap-time master equation (TUM/Heilmeier): t_lap = t_q + t_gap_racepace + t_car + m_fuel*t_lap_sens_mass + t_tire(age) + DRS/grid/start/traffic terms
Fuel sensitivity t_lap_sens_mass = 0.03 s/kg typical (~0.3 s per 10 kg); track range 0.019 (Spielberg) to 0.036 (Yas Marina) s/kg
Starting fuel mass m_fuel = 110 kg (105 kg in 2017 config); F1 max tank 110 kg
Fuel burn b_fuel_perlap = 1.55-2.0 kg/lap (1.549, 1.909, 2.0 in TUM configs); independent analyses use ~1.6-1.8 kg/lap
Linear tyre deg: t_tire = k_0 + k_1_lin*age ; k_1_lin = 0.026-0.079 s/lap normal compounds, up to 0.186 s/lap softest (TUM Yas Marina 2019)
Quadratic: t_tire = k_0 + k_1_quad*age + k_2_quad*age^2 ; k_2_quad ~ 0.0001-0.0067 s/lap^2 (TUM)
Logarithmic (best per Heilmeier 2020a): t_tire = k_0 + k_1_ln*ln(k_2_ln*age + 1)
Cubic: t_tire = k_0 + k_1_cub*age + k_2_cub*age^2 + k_3_cub*age^3
k_0 = fresh-tyre compound pace offset; adjacent-compound delta ~0.5 s/lap (Austria 2025 state-space: hard 69.5s, med 69.0s, soft 68.5s)
FIA target compound deltas: medium 1.2 s/lap faster than hard, soft 2.2 s/lap faster; real 2023 closer (~0.5s M-H, ~1.0s S-H)
State-space degradation estimate (Hamilton, Austria 2025): nu = 0.054 s/lap (hard), 0.060 s/lap (medium), CIs +/-0.004-0.009; compound difference not statistically significant
Cold/un-warmed out-lap penalty t_add_coldtires = 1.0 s
Degradation multiplier under Safety Car = 0.25, under FCY/VSC = 0.5 (tyre 'ages' fractionally)
Pit standstill = t_pit_tirechange_min 1.9 s + team add 0.43-1.37 s; pit drive-through loss ~11.4 s (Spielberg) to ~18 s (Yas Marina)
SC base lap-time multiplier 1.6 (+60%), FCY/VSC multiplier 1.4 (+40%)
FIA deg target: ~2 s total drop by 22% race distance (hard), 18% (medium), 10% (soft)
Real 2024 Bahrain test wear: 0.1-0.2 s/lap; healthy hard stint ~0.05 s/lap, struggling stint 0.15+ s/lap
findings.modelling_recommendation: Adopt the Heilmeier/TUM lap-wise additive structure as the backbone: lap_time(driver, lap) = t_base + t_car_driver + fuel_mass(lap)*k_fuel + t_tire(compound, tyre_age) + situational. (1) FUEL: track fuel mass linearly: fuel_mass(lap) = m_fuel_start - burn_per_lap*lap, t_fuel = fuel_mass*k_fuel with k_fuel = 0.03 s/kg default (tune 0.02-0.04 per track), m_fuel_start = 110 kg, burn_per_lap = total_fuel/n_laps (clamp >= ~1.6 kg/lap). Because start fuel is fixed and known, you can equivalently fuel-correct observed data by ADDING back k_fuel*burn_per_lap*(laps_remaining) to compare stints. (2) TYRE: use the quadratic form t_tire = k_0 + k_1*age + k_2*age^2 as the practical default - it captures gentle degradation plus a softening 'cliff' onset; reserve the logarithmic form k_0 + k_1_ln*ln(k_2_ln*age+1) if you can fit warm-up curvature with good data (Heilmeier found it superior). Pure linear (k_0 + k_1*age) is the safe fallback when data is sparse. Per-compound: set k_0 to the fresh-tyre offset (soft ~ -0.5 to -1.0 s vs medium, hard ~ +0.5 s vs medium), and increase k_1 going softer (e.g. hard ~0.03, medium ~0.045, soft ~0.06-0.09 s/lap; softest cliff compounds up to ~0.18). (3) WARM-UP/CLIFF: add a one-off cold-tyre out-lap penalty of ~1.0 s on the first lap of each stint; optionally let the first 1-3 laps have reduced/negative effective degradation to model warm-up (the state-space study found nu starts negative). Model the cliff either by the quadratic curvature or a hard threshold beyond which k_1 jumps - do NOT rely on a single linear slope through the whole stint. (4) GRAINING/THERMAL: don't add separate closed-form terms for a first version; instead absorb them into per-event, per-compound k_1/k_2 fits from FP2 long-runs, and flag overheating-prone tracks/compounds with steeper slopes and earlier cliff onset. (5) SC/VSC: scale degradation accrual by 0.25 (SC) / 0.5 (VSC) and inflate base lap time by 1.6x / 1.4x. (6) PIT LOSS: split into standstill (~1.9 s + ~0.5 s team) and pit-lane drive-through (track-specific 11-23 s). GOTCHAS: t_lap_sens_mass is strongly track-dependent (0.019 at short tracks vs 0.036 at long ones) - don't hardcode one value; the cliff is the main reason linear models mis-predict late-stint pace; compound degradation deltas are often statistically indistinct in clean data, so calibrate to long-run telemetry rather than assuming large fixed gaps; FastF1 lap data needs SC/VSC/in-lap/out-lap filtering before fitting. For probabilistic strategy use, add a Gaussian per-lap noise (sigma ~0.1-0.3 s) or the skewed-t error from the state-space paper to model driver-mistake outliers.

findings.topic: F1 pit-stop time loss and undercut/overcut/double-stack mechanics for a race strategy simulator

key_findings.claim: Total pit lane time loss (delta vs staying out) is typically ~20-25s, with outliers from ~18s up to ~28-30s depending on pit lane length and speed limit
key_findings.detail: This is the full in-lap-to-out-lap delta: time entering pit lane, decelerating to the speed limit, the stationary stop, accelerating, and rejoining, MINUS what the car would have done staying at racing speed. Driven mainly by pit lane length and speed limit (80 km/h standard, 60 km/h at Monaco/Singapore). Low-loss circuits like COTA/Austin sit under ~20s; high-loss circuits like Singapore and Imola reach ~27-30s because of long pit lanes and/or 60 km/h limits.
key_findings.numbers: Typical 20-25s; range ~18s (low) to ~28-30s (high). Monaco ~20s; Barcelona/Silverstone ~21-25s; Bahrain ~22-24s; Monza ~24s; Singapore/Imola ~27-30s

key_findings.claim: Per-circuit pit-lane delta correlates with pit lane length and speed limit; Monaco is short, Silverstone/Imola/Interlagos are long
key_findings.detail: Monaco pit lane ~305m (one of shortest), Silverstone ~457m, Albert Park ~281m, Interlagos ~1140m / Imola among longest. Monaco still loses ~20s despite short length because of its 60 km/h limit. Use this to derive per-track values: longer pit lane and/or lower limit = larger delta. Singapore quoted at ~27-28s partly due to 60 km/h limit.
key_findings.numbers: Pit lane lengths: Albert Park ~281m, Monaco ~305m, Silverstone ~457m, Interlagos ~1140m. Speed limits: 80 km/h standard, 60 km/h Monaco/Singapore

key_findings.claim: Stationary (four-tyre-change) time is ~2.0-3.5s for a normal stop; top teams routinely 2.0-2.5s; record 1.80s
key_findings.detail: A clean top-team stop is 2.0-2.5s stationary. A slightly fumbled or lower-midfield stop pushes toward 3.0-3.5s. The official world record is 1.80s (McLaren, 2023 Qatar GP); Red Bull set 1.82s at 2019 Brazil. A bad wheel-gun/cross-thread issue can add ~4s (e.g. Vettel left-front at 2020 Abu Dhabi cost ~4s extra). Note the stationary time is a SMALL part of the total pit delta — most of the ~20-25s is the slow pit-lane transit.
key_findings.numbers: Normal 2.0-3.5s; top team 2.0-2.5s; record 1.80s; world-record-pace 1.82s; botched stop adds ~4s

key_findings.claim: A typical undercut gives ~1s/lap of fresh-vs-old tyre advantage (up to ~1.5-2s on the out-lap), and pays off over ~2-3 laps
key_findings.detail: Fresh tyres are worth roughly 1s per lap versus worn tyres in steady state, and as much as 1.5-2s on the first flying out-lap once they are up to temperature (Pirelli tyres warm up within a corner or two). To complete an undercut you must build a gap larger than the time your rival will lose in their own stop; because the per-lap advantage is ~1s and the pit delta is ~20-25s, the undercut only works when you are already within ~1-2s of the rival on track, and it 'pays off' (you emerge ahead) over the ~2-3 laps spanning your stop and theirs. On high-deg tracks (Barcelona, Silverstone) the swing can be 3s+ over just two laps.
key_findings.numbers: Fresh-tyre advantage ~1s/lap (steady), ~1.5-2s on out-lap; pays off over ~2-3 laps; needs to be within ~1-2s of rival; up to 3s over 2 laps on high-deg tracks

key_findings.claim: The overcut works in low-degradation, slow-warmup, or track-position-critical situations
key_findings.detail: Overcut = stay out longer than your rival, run in clear air after they pit, then pit later and emerge ahead. Favoured when: (a) tyre degradation is low so staying out costs little lap time; (b) the rival's fresh tyres warm up slowly so their out-lap is weak; (c) track position is extremely valuable / overtaking is hard (Monaco-type); (d) pitting would release the rival into backmarker traffic; (e) tyres are in a 'sweet-spot' plateau phase where old-tyre pace is stable. In modern F1 the overcut is more situational than the undercut because Pirelli tyres warm up fast, reducing the slow-out-lap window the overcut exploits.
key_findings.numbers: No single number; condition-based. Relies on old-tyre pace deficit being < fresh-tyre warmup deficit over the swing laps

key_findings.claim: Double-stacking costs the second car ~2-4s of extra waiting (more if the first stop goes wrong)
key_findings.detail: Double-stack = pitting both team cars on consecutive same-lap stops. The pit crew can only service one car at a time, so the second car must wait roughly the duration of one stop (~2-3s) for the box to clear, effectively adding ~2-4s to the second car's stop. If the first car's stop is slow or has a problem, that delay compounds onto the second car. Teams want the second car ~4-6s behind the first on entry to avoid a queue; double-stacks are most common under Safety Car/VSC when the field is bunched and pit-delta cost is reduced.
key_findings.numbers: Second car waits ~2-4s extra (≈ one stop duration); recommended gap ~4-6s behind first car on pit entry

concrete_numbers: Total pit-lane time loss (delta vs staying out): typical 20-25s; full range ~18s to ~30s
Per-circuit pit loss estimates: Monaco ~20s, Barcelona ~21-23s, Silverstone ~21-25s, Bahrain ~22-24s, Monza ~24s, Singapore/Imola ~27-30s
Pit-lane speed limit: 80 km/h standard, 60 km/h at Monaco and Singapore
Stationary 4-tyre change: normal 2.0-3.5s; top-team clean 2.0-2.5s; world record 1.80s (McLaren, 2023 Qatar); 1.82s (Red Bull, 2019 Brazil)
Botched stop penalty: ~+4s (e.g. Vettel left-front, 2020 Abu Dhabi)
Fresh-vs-old tyre advantage: ~1.0s/lap steady-state; ~1.5-2.0s on the out-lap; up to ~3s over 2 laps on high-deg tracks
Undercut trigger window: must be within ~1-2s of rival; pays off over ~2-3 laps
Double-stack penalty for 2nd car: ~+2-4s wait (≈ one stop duration); want ~4-6s gap on entry
Pit lane lengths: Albert Park ~281m, Monaco ~305m, Silverstone ~457m, Interlagos ~1140m
findings.modelling_recommendation: Model pit loss as a per-circuit constant PIT_LOSS[track] (seconds) representing the in-lap+out-lap delta vs staying out. Default ~22s; set Monaco ~20, Barcelona ~22, Silverstone ~23, Bahrain ~23, Monza ~24, Singapore/Imola ~28. If you want to derive it: PIT_LOSS ≈ stationary_time + 2 * (pit_lane_length / pit_speed_limit_m_per_s - pit_lane_length / racing_speed_m_per_s)-ish transit penalty; simpler to just hardcode per-track. Separate the stationary component: STATIONARY = normal(mean=2.4s, with a small tail to 3.5s; occasional botch +4s) and fold it into PIT_LOSS so total = transit_delta + stationary. For tyre/undercut model: give each compound a pace curve where a fresh set is ~1.0s/lap faster than a same-compound set near the end of its stint, plus a one-off out-lap bonus of ~1.0-1.5s once warmed (warmup ~1 lap). Undercut emerges naturally: simulate driver A pitting lap N (loses PIT_LOSS but gains fresh-tyre delta each subsequent lap) and driver B pitting lap N+k; A passes B if accumulated fresh-tyre gain over k laps exceeds the on-track gap A conceded. Because gain is ~1s/lap, undercut succeeds within ~1-2s and resolves over 2-3 laps. Overcut: make old-tyre pace degradation gentle (low deg) and add a cold-tyre out-lap PENALTY to the pitting car (~1-1.5s) so staying out can win when deg is low or warmup penalty is high — gate it on track-position value (penalise on-track passing difficulty per circuit). Double-stack: when both cars pit same lap, add a queue penalty to the 2nd car = max(0, first_car_stationary_time) ≈ +2.5s default, compounding if the first stop is slow. Make double-stacks attractive under SC/VSC by reducing effective PIT_LOSS (field bunched, pit-lane transit relatively cheaper) — a common simplification is SC pit loss ≈ 40-60% of green-flag pit loss. Gotchas: stationary time is only ~10% of total pit loss, so don't let pit-crew speed dominate strategy; the dominant lever is per-circuit transit delta and tyre deg rate. Treat all single numbers as ranges, not exact — confidence on per-circuit values is medium (mostly secondary/aggregator sources, not official FIA pit-delta tables).

findings.topic: Safety Car (SC) and Virtual Safety Car (VSC) statistics and their effect on F1 race strategy, for a Monte Carlo race simulator

key_findings.claim: The TUM/Heilmeier open-source F1 race simulator is the authoritative reference and gives the full stochastic SC/VSC model with fitted historical probabilities (seasons 2014-2019).
key_findings.detail: From pars_mcs.ini [ALL_SEASONS]: number of SC phases per race is drawn from p_sc_quant = [0.455, 0.413, 0.099, 0.033] for [0,1,2,3] SCs. This implies P(>=1 full SC in a race) = 0.545 (54.5%) and E[number of SC phases] = 0.71. SC start lap distribution p_sc_start = [0.364, 0.136, 0.136, 0.080, 0.193, 0.091] over [lap1, <20%, <40%, <60%, <80%, <100% race distance] (note strong lap-1 spike and a late-race bump). SC duration distribution p_sc_duration over 1-10 laps = [0, 0.182, 0.25, 0.227, 0.193, 0.057, 0.068, 0.023, 0, 0] giving E[SC duration] ~ 4.0 laps. VSC modelled as: after each driver retirement-by-failure, a VSC is triggered with p_vsc_aft_failure = 0.227; VSC duration over 1-4 laps p_vsc_duration = [0.479, 0.396, 0.021, 0.104], E ~ 1.75 laps.
key_findings.numbers: P(>=1 SC)=54.5%; E[#SC/race]=0.71; SC duration mean ~4 laps (mode 2-3); P(VSC | a failure)=0.227; VSC duration mean ~1.75 laps; SC quant dist [0.455,0.413,0.099,0.033]

key_findings.claim: Lap-time multipliers: SC laps run at ~160% of green lap time; VSC (FCY) laps at ~140%.
key_findings.detail: Track parameter files set mult_t_lap_sc = 1.6 and mult_t_lap_fcy = 1.4 for every circuit; the source code calc_racetimes_basic.py hard-codes the same fallback: 't_lap_sc = t_base * 1.6' and t_lap_fcy = 1.4. The f1metrics simulator independently uses ~140% of normal lap time at full SC pace and ~120% during the delta/forming phase. Practitioner articles quote cars slowing 'roughly 40%' under SC/VSC, consistent with the 1.4-1.6x band.
key_findings.numbers: SC lap = 1.6x green (+60%); VSC lap = 1.4x green (+40%). f1metrics: SC pace ~1.4x, delta phase ~1.2x.

key_findings.claim: Pitting under SC/VSC is a 'cheap stop': on-track time lost while pitting drops by roughly 40-80% vs green, with full SC cheaper than VSC. Absolute saving is typically ~7-12 seconds.
key_findings.detail: From the simulator's per-track pit-drive loss params (in-lap + out-lap driving loss, excluding the near-constant pit-lane stationary/speed-limit time): Red Bull Ring 2016 green=14.1s, VSC=4.0s (save 10.1s/71%), SC=2.5s (save 11.6s/82%); Silverstone 2017 green=17.0s, VSC=7.2s (save 9.8s/58%), SC=5.4s (save 11.6s/68%); Baku 2018 green=17.1s, VSC=10.2s (save 6.9s/40%), SC=7.2s (save 9.9s/58%). Practitioner consensus: a normal stop costs ~20-25s (range 18-28s); under VSC you save ~30-40% of that loss, under full SC ~40-60% (e.g. a 22s stop drops to ~12-14s). Mercedes reported saving ~10-11s by pitting under SC. Monaco-specific analysis cites a ~7s saving as the decisive strategic number.
key_findings.numbers: Green pit loss ~20-25s (range 18-28s). VSC saves ~30-40% of loss; SC saves ~40-60% (commonly stated ~50%). Absolute saving ~7-12s. Effective SC stop ~10-14s.

key_findings.claim: Recent full-season counts give ~1.2-1.8 neutralisations per race and ~75-90% of races with at least one SC or VSC.
key_findings.detail: 2022: 39 caution periods over 22 races = 25 SC + 18 VSC; 20 of 22 races (91%) had at least one SC or VSC; only Spain and Abu Dhabi were clean (1.77 cautions/race). 2024: 17 SC + 10 VSC = 27 neutralisations over 24 races; 12 races had >=1 SC (50%), 9 had >=1 VSC; note a record 9-race run with no full SC. The 54.5% P(>=1 SC) from the 2014-2019 fit sits between the 2024 (50%) and higher-incident seasons; combined SC-or-VSC per-race probability is materially higher (~75-90%).
key_findings.numbers: 2022: 1.77 cautions/race, 91% of races with SC or VSC, 25 SC / 18 VSC. 2024: 1.13/race, 27 total (17 SC, 10 VSC), 50% of races with a full SC.

key_findings.claim: Circuit-specific SC probability varies enormously: Singapore ~near-100%, Baku ~86%, Monaco ~21-29%, Monza ~27%, Paul Ricard as low as ~10%.
key_findings.detail: Singapore (Marina Bay) had at least one SC in EVERY race from 2008 until the streak broke in 2024 (~100% historically, 24 SC deployments). Baku/Azerbaijan quoted at ~86% SC chance (only the 2016 inaugural race had no SC or VSC; one summary gives 57% full-SC over 7 races plus frequent VSCs). Monaco: 15 of ~70 races had a SC (~21%); since 2018, VSC in 43% of Monaco GPs, full SC in 29%, red flag in 29% (clean races are the exception); 2021/2023/2024 had none. Monza: ~27% SC probability (only ~9 Italian GPs since 2000 had a SC) - a notably LOW track. Canada/Gilles Villeneuve is the highest-frequency permanent-ish circuit (~37+ SC deployments). Street/tight circuits (Singapore, Baku, Monaco, Jeddah) skew high; fast open circuits with big run-off (Monza, Paul Ricard, Spain) skew low.

key_findings.claim: Standard practice for modelling SC arrival is a per-lap hazard / Poisson-style process, often coupled to retirements; teams run 10,000+ Monte Carlo race draws.
key_findings.detail: Two common approaches: (1) Per-lap hazard: each lap has a probability p that a SC is triggered (illustratively ~10%/lap on a SC-prone track), equivalent to a discrete-time Poisson/Bernoulli arrival process; expected count and timing follow from the per-lap rate. (2) Retirement-coupled (Heilmeier): first draw the NUMBER of SC phases for the race from a categorical distribution (p_sc_quant), then place each phase's start lap by sampling from an empirical start-distribution, then sample duration; accidents trigger SC and failures trigger VSC with probability 0.227. Both feed a Monte Carlo loop of thousands of races to build outcome distributions per strategy. f1metrics couples SC issuance to a driver retirement event, with per-track historical SC likelihood. For a simple simulator, a constant per-lap hazard lambda calibrated so that 1-exp(-lambda*N_laps) equals the track's historical P(>=1 SC) is a clean, defensible choice.
key_findings.numbers: Per-lap SC hazard illustratively ~0.10 on SC-prone tracks; calibrate lambda via P(>=1 SC)=1-exp(-lambda*N_laps); 10,000+ MC race draws typical; Heilmeier number-of-SC categorical [0.455,0.413,0.099,0.033]

findings.modelling_recommendation: Model SC and VSC as separate stochastic processes feeding a per-lap discrete simulation, calibrated per circuit. RECOMMENDED (Heilmeier/TUM approach, best validated): (1) Draw the number of SC phases for the race from a categorical distribution; default [P0,P1,P2,P3]=[0.455,0.413,0.099,0.033], but scale to the circuit's historical P(>=1 SC) (Singapore ~1.0, Baku ~0.86, Monaco ~0.25, Monza ~0.27, Paul Ricard ~0.10). (2) For each SC, sample a start lap using the empirical weights [lap1=0.364, then 0.136/0.136/0.080/0.193/0.091 spread across the <20/40/60/80/100% race-distance bins] - note the lap-1 spike and a late-race bump. (3) Sample SC duration from the 1-10 lap pmf [0,0.182,0.25,0.227,0.193,0.057,0.068,0.023,0,0] (mean ~4 laps). (4) VSC: per modelled driver retirement-from-failure, trigger a VSC with prob 0.227; sample VSC duration from 1-4 laps [0.479,0.396,0.021,0.104] (mean ~1.75). SIMPLER ALTERNATIVE: a constant per-lap Bernoulli/Poisson hazard lambda chosen so 1-exp(-lambda*N_laps) equals the circuit's historical P(>=1 SC); each arrival becomes an SC (prob ~0.55) or VSC (~0.45). LAP-TIME EFFECT: multiply the green lap time by 1.6 during SC laps and 1.4 during VSC laps (optionally model a slower 1-lap 'forming/bunch-up' transition at ~1.2x like f1metrics). During neutralisation, scale tyre degradation and fuel use down (x0.25 under SC, x0.5 under VSC). PIT 'CHEAP STOP': split pit loss into a fixed pit-lane component (stationary + speed-limited travel, roughly constant) and a variable on-track time-loss-to-the-field component. Under SC reduce the effective loss by ~50% (range 40-60%), under VSC by ~30-40%; in absolute terms a ~20-25s green loss becomes ~10-14s. Implement this as loss_eff = green_loss * (1 - saving_frac) with saving_frac ~ 0.50 (SC) / 0.35 (VSC), or use per-track in/out-lap deltas if you have them. GOTCHAS: SCs cluster on lap 1 and late in the race (not uniform) - a flat hazard underweights both; full SC bunches the field (closes gaps, big positional swing) whereas VSC preserves gaps (smaller positional gain) so the value of a stop differs even at equal time saved; VSC can end with only ~10-15s warning, so a perfect-information sim overvalues VSC stops; the simulator's per-track pit-drive numbers exclude the fixed pit-lane time, so don't double-count. Wrap all of this in a 10,000+ iteration Monte Carlo loop to get an outcome distribution per strategy.

findings.topic: How F1 race-strategy simulators model overtaking, dirty air, DRS, and track position (with concrete parameters from the Heilmeier/TUM, f1metrics, and Sulsters models)

key_findings.claim: Overtaking is modelled as a per-lap pace-delta threshold: the trailing car only passes if it is faster than the car ahead by a circuit-specific 'overtaking gap' (t_gap_overtake). In the canonical TUM/Heilmeier sim this gap ranges ~1.26 s (easiest) to 3.75 s (hardest) per lap.
key_findings.detail: TUMFTM/race-simulation computes each driver's cumulative race time at lap end; for an adjacent pair the trailing car overtakes only if its time advantage >= t_gap_overtake_tot. Code (racesim/src/race.py L942): `if overtake_allowed and racetimes_tmp[pos_cur_b] - racetimes_tmp[pos_back_b] >= t_gap_overtake_tot`. t_gap_overtake_tot = track.t_gap_overtake + velocity-delta modifier + team-order modifier. Verified by cloning the repo and reading the .ini parameter files plus race.py.
key_findings.numbers: t_gap_overtake per circuit (2019 .ini files): Suzuka 1.26 s, Silverstone 1.35 s, Sakhir/Bahrain 1.38 s, Shanghai 1.50 s, Hockenheim 1.56 s, Baku 1.62 s, Le Castellet 1.635 s, Monza 1.755 s, Austin 1.83 s, Spa 1.83 s, Spielberg 2.01 s, Sao Paulo 2.025 s, Mexico City 2.055 s, Yas Marina 2.07 s, Sochi 2.13 s, Catalunya 2.31 s, Budapest 2.415 s, Melbourne 2.70 s, Monte Carlo (Monaco) 3.75 s, Montreal 3.75 s, Singapore 3.75 s

key_findings.claim: The per-circuit overtaking gap IS the 'overtaking difficulty' ranking. Monaco (Monte Carlo), Singapore and Montreal are hardest (3.75 s required advantage = effectively unpassable on pace); Suzuka, Silverstone and Bahrain (Sakhir) are easiest (~1.26-1.38 s).
key_findings.detail: This directly answers the per-circuit ranking ask. The values were tuned by Heilmeier et al. to reproduce historical overtaking counts. Monaco's 3.75 s means a car must be ~3.75 s/lap faster to clear the car ahead, which essentially never happens on equal cars - matching real-world Monaco being a procession. The threshold is reduced by t_gap_overtake_vel (~-0.03 s per km/h of top-speed delta), so a big straight-line speed advantage lowers the required gap.
key_findings.numbers: Hardest: Monaco 3.75 / Singapore 3.75 / Montreal 3.75 s. Mid: Monza 1.755 s. Easiest: Suzuka 1.26 / Silverstone 1.35 / Bahrain 1.38 s. Velocity modifier t_gap_overtake_vel approx -0.031 to -0.061 s per km/h top-speed difference (negative = lowers threshold).

key_findings.claim: DRS is modelled as a fixed negative lap-time bonus applied when the trailing car is within a 1.0 s window of the car ahead, enabled only from a start-of-race lap onward and disabled for a few laps after a safety car.
key_findings.detail: TUM model: use_drs=true, drs_window=1.0 s, drs_allow_lap=3, drs_sc_delay=2 laps. The bonus t_drseffect (negative) is split in half across the lap (race.py L641-655: `self.laptimes[...] += self.track.t_drseffect / 2.0` applied twice). f1metrics uses a net DRS gain of -0.4 s/lap, granted from lap 3 to a car within 1.0 s at lap start. Sulsters thesis uses tDRS = -0.5 s with a 1.0 s DRS threshold, DRS blocked for the first two laps and during safety car.
key_findings.numbers: TUM t_drseffect per circuit ranged approx -0.13 s (Montreal) to -0.92 s (Singapore); typical ~-0.46 to -0.55 s/lap (e.g. Monza -0.462, Bahrain -0.532, Catalunya -0.756). f1metrics: -0.4 s/lap net. Sulsters: -0.5 s/lap. DRS window = 1.0 s in all three.

key_findings.claim: Overall overtaking threshold rule of thumb used by teams and the f1metrics sim: you need to be roughly 1 s/lap faster even WITH DRS, i.e. ~0.8 s/lap faster in clean air without DRS, to actually pass at most circuits.
key_findings.detail: f1metrics: author 'guesstimated a threshold of 1.2 s', meaning the driver must be a net 0.8 s/lap quicker in clean air without DRS (because the 0.4 s DRS gain plus reaching the threshold closes the gap). Threshold adjusted by 0.2 s for every 10 km/h of straight-line-speed difference. Aston Martin's strategist (Tom McCullough) independently states the team 'overtaking threshold' is about a second a lap faster even with DRS at most circuits.
key_findings.numbers: Overtaking threshold ~1.2 s/lap (f1metrics), equivalent to ~0.8 s/lap clean-air advantage without DRS; +/-0.2 s per 10 km/h straight-line speed delta; team rule of thumb ~1 s/lap even with DRS.

key_findings.claim: Time lost stuck behind a slower car is modelled by a minimum-gap constraint plus per-lap penalties, not a single fixed number: the follower is clamped to a minimum gap (0.2-0.5 s) behind the leader, and both cars take a 'duel' time loss each lap they fight (~0.3 s) and an extra loss when a pass finally happens (~0.3-0.5 s for the overtaken car).
key_findings.detail: TUM: min_t_dist = 0.5 s (0.8 s under safety car); a follower cannot be placed closer than this, so its effective lap time is inflated to sit 0.5 s behind (race.py L962-968). t_duel = 0.3 s/lap applied to both cars when within min_t_dist and a pass is allowed. t_overtake_loser = 0.3 s added to the lap time of the car that gets passed. f1metrics: minimum gap 0.2 s, and a 0.4 s loss for the overtaken car. Net effect: a car genuinely faster than the one ahead but below the overtaking threshold simply circulates ~0.5 s behind, bleeding all its surplus pace = the 'track-position is king' result. This is how the sims value track position: a faster car can be trapped indefinitely, losing its entire pace advantage each lap, which is why undercut/overcut pit strategy is used to gain position instead of on-track passing.
key_findings.numbers: TUM: min_t_dist 0.5 s (0.8 s under SC), t_duel 0.3 s/lap, t_overtake_loser 0.3 s. f1metrics: min gap 0.2 s, overtaken-car loss 0.4 s. Sulsters: min gap (delta_min) 0.2 s, overtaking penalty 0.5 s.

key_findings.claim: Dirty-air / following pace penalty is modelled two ways: (a) increased tyre wear when running close (f1metrics: tyre-wear rate x1.1 on any lap spent within ~1 s), and (b) a direct lap-time penalty that is a linear function of gap, active only for gaps roughly 0.2-1.5 s, downforce-dominated (a loss) at high-downforce tracks and drag-dominated (a gain/slipstream) at low-downforce tracks.
key_findings.detail: f1metrics applies a 1.1x tyre-wear multiplier whenever a car is close enough to get the DRS/dirty-air flag, so the cost of following is paid in accelerated degradation rather than a fixed lap-time hit. The 2026 multi-agent TUM-lineage paper (arXiv 2602.23056) models the aerodynamic interaction as Delta_T_int = a*t_gap + b for t_gap in [0.2 s, 1.5 s], else 0, with a < 0 (penalty grows as gap shrinks). At Bahrain (downforce-limited, many corners) following is a net lap-time LOSS; at Monza (drag-limited) the slipstream is a net GAIN. Public sources give the underlying aero loss in downforce-% rather than a single canonical s/lap figure, so the exact seconds/lap is model-dependent.
key_findings.numbers: f1metrics tyre-wear penalty: x1.1 when within DRS/dirty-air range. Multi-agent model: linear penalty over gap window 0.2-1.5 s, sign flips by circuit (Bahrain loss, Monza gain). Effective held-up cost in TUM sim ~0.5 s/lap via min_t_dist clamp.

key_findings.claim: Ground-effect (2022+) era dirty-air specifics: the 2022 rules cut following downforce loss dramatically vs 2021, but it has steadily regressed back toward pre-2022 levels by 2024-2025 as teams developed outwash.
key_findings.detail: Pre-2022 (2021 cars): ~35% downforce lost at ~20 m (≈3 car lengths), ~47% lost at ~10 m (≈1 car length). 2022 launch spec: only ~4-5% lost at 20 m, ~18-20% lost at 10 m. By 2023-2025 it had worsened to ~35% loss when close (one car length) and retention figures fell - The Race CFD data: at 10 m downforce retained dropped from 85% (2022) to 65% (2025); at 20 m from 95% (2022) to 80% (2025). FIA target for 2026 cars ~18% loss at 0.5 s behind. Translating % downforce loss to s/lap is circuit-specific and not published as one number; sims encode it via the tyre-wear factor or the gap-dependent linear penalty above.
key_findings.numbers: 2021: ~35% DF loss at 20 m, ~47% at 10 m. 2022 launch: ~4-5% at 20 m, ~18-20% at 10 m. 2023-25: ~20% (2022) rising to >30-35% close; The Race: 10 m retention 85%->65%, 20 m retention 95%->80% (2022->2025). 2026 FIA target ~18% loss at 0.5 s.

key_findings.claim: Overtaking probability is an explicit, per-circuit calibrated parameter in some sims (Sulsters/Bekker-Lotz lineage): a pass that clears the threshold still only succeeds with probability p_overtaking, tuned so simulated overtake counts match reality.
key_findings.detail: Sulsters thesis (which builds directly on f1metrics parameters) makes the pass probabilistic: overtaking threshold alpha_overtaking and overtaking probability p_overtaking are tuned per race by matching simulated vs actual overtake counts over 1000 sims. Harder tracks get a larger (more negative) threshold and lower probability; easier tracks the reverse. The TUM/Heilmeier model is instead deterministic on pace (no p_overtaking) but adds Monte-Carlo randomness elsewhere. Context: DRS introduction in 2011 raised average overtakes per race from 28.79 (2010) to 60.63 (2011).
key_findings.numbers: Sulsters calibrated values: Japan threshold -1.9 s, p=0.18; USA -1.8 s, p=0.40; Mexico -1.9 s, p=0.10; Abu Dhabi -1.5 s, p=0.30. Fixed: tDRS -0.5 s, DRS threshold 1.0 s, overtaking penalty 0.5 s, min gap 0.2 s. Calibration target overtakes: Mexico ~25 (low), USA ~57 (high). DRS effect on overtakes/race: 28.79 (2010) -> 60.63 (2011).
