findings.modelling_recommendation: Model overtaking lap-by-lap on cumulative race time (the Heilmeier/TUM approach), not continuous position. Per lap: (1) sort cars by cumulative time; (2) for each adjacent pair compute the trailing car's time advantage; (3) a pass occurs only if advantage >= t_gap_overtake (the per-circuit difficulty number) minus a small straight-line-speed term (~0.03 s/km/h of top-speed delta). Use the TUM per-circuit table directly as your overtaking-difficulty parameter: ~1.3 s for easy tracks (Bahrain, Silverstone, Suzuka), ~1.75 s mid (Monza), 3.75 s for Monaco/Singapore/Montreal (effectively unpassable on pace). For a stochastic flavour, gate the pass behind an overtaking-probability p (Sulsters: 0.1-0.4, lower on hard tracks). Track position 'value' emerges automatically from a minimum-gap clamp: if a faster car is below the threshold, hold it at min_t_dist (0.5 s) behind and inflate its lap time accordingly, plus add a per-lap duel penalty (0.3 s) - this makes a trapped faster car bleed its entire pace surplus each lap and is what drives undercut/overcut pit strategy. DRS: grant a fixed bonus (-0.4 to -0.5 s/lap) when the gap is within 1.0 s at lap start, only from lap 3 and not for ~2 laps after a safety car; this lowers the effective threshold so a within-DRS car needs ~0.8 s/lap raw pace to clear. Dirty air: cheapest realistic model is f1metrics' tyre-wear multiplier (x1.1 while within ~1 s) so following costs degradation rather than instantaneous time; a more physical option (multi-agent TUM paper) is a gap-dependent linear lap-time delta active only between 0.2-1.5 s, with the SIGN set per circuit - a penalty at high-downforce tracks (Bahrain/Monaco) and a small slipstream BENEFIT at low-downforce tracks (Monza). For the 2022+ ground-effect era, scale the dirty-air penalty down vs the pre-2022 era but note it has crept back up by 2024-25; treat the magnitude as a tunable parameter calibrated to historical overtake counts rather than a fixed published s/lap, because public data is in downforce-% not seconds. Apply a small fixed penalty (~0.3-0.5 s) to the overtaken car the lap a pass completes to ease multi-car passing and avoid oscillation/infinite-loop swaps (the TUM code explicitly guards against re-passing loops when t_overtake_loser is too small).

findings.topic: Optimizing F1 race strategy (pit timing, number of stops, tire compounds) under uncertainty: Monte Carlo simulation, dynamic programming/exhaustive enumeration, robust vs expected-value optimization, RL, and real-time safety-car re-optimization

key_findings.claim: The de-facto open-source reference is the TUM FTM 'race-simulation' (Heilmeier et al.). It splits into a deterministic/exhaustive optimizer (racesim_basic) for free-track strategy and a multi-agent Monte Carlo simulator (racesim) for probabilistic robustness evaluation. It is lap-discretized (one timestep = one lap) for speed, and ships .ini parameter files for 121 F1 races (2014-2019).
key_findings.detail: racesim_basic does exhaustive enumeration assuming no competitors; racesim adds car-to-car interactions (overtaking, traffic), random failures, FCY/SC phases via a 'ghost car', starting-performance scatter and lap-time noise. Mode is chosen by no_sim_runs: ==1 gives a single deterministic race exported to CSV; >1 triggers Monte Carlo with mcs_analysis() producing histograms/distributions of finishing time and position. The whole thing is open source (MIT-style) and directly implementable in Python/NumPy.
key_findings.numbers: 121 race param sets (2014-2019); lap-wise discretization; multi-process up to 200 concurrent jobs

key_findings.claim: Lap time is an additive model: T_lap = t_base + fuel-mass term + tire-degradation term + pit/FCY/SC/DRS corrections + Gaussian noise. This is the standard functional form across the literature and is what you should implement.
key_findings.detail: From the Spielberg 2019 param file: base = qualifying time t_q plus a race-pace gap (t_q=63.003 s, t_gap_racepace=4.036 s). Fuel effect = t_lap_sens_mass * current_fuel_mass with t_lap_sens_mass=0.019 s per kg; fuel burns at b_fuel_perlap=1.549 kg/lap from m_fuel=110 kg at start (so a full tank costs ~2.1 s/lap, decaying to 0). DRS gives t_drseffect=-0.322 s. Tire degradation is a per-compound polynomial in tire age (laps) selectable as lin/quad/cub/ln: linear t_tire = k_0 + k_1_lin*age; quadratic t_tire = k_0 + k_1_quad*age + k_2_quad*age^2. Example (Hamilton, Spielberg): soft k_0=0.0384, k_1=0.0232 s/lap; medium k_1=0.0167 s/lap; hard k_1=0.0100 s/lap; quadratic k_2 ~ 0.0001-0.0007 s/lap^2. Gaussian lap-time noise sigma is driver-specific, ~0.46-0.86 s.
key_findings.numbers: t_q=63.003s; t_gap_racepace=4.036s; t_lap_sens_mass=0.019 s/kg; b_fuel_perlap=1.549 kg/lap; m_fuel=110 kg; DRS=-0.322s; soft k_1=0.0232, med 0.0167, hard 0.0100 s/lap; lap noise sigma 0.46-0.86s

key_findings.claim: Pit-stop time loss is modeled as in-lap loss + standstill (tire change) + out-lap loss, totalling roughly 20-22 s on a free track, and is HALVED (~10 s) under a safety car because the field is already running slow. This SC effect is the single most important strategic lever and must be in the model.
key_findings.detail: Spielberg 2019: t_pit_tirechange_min=1.9 s standstill (plus 0.43-1.37 s team-specific), t_pitdrive_inlap=2.691 s, t_pitdrive_outlap=11.396 s -> combined drive-through ~14.1 s plus standstill ~ total ~16-22 s. Industry rule of thumb: ~20 s normal pit loss, ~10 s under SC. Under SC the per-lap time itself is scaled by mult_t_lap_sc=1.6; under VSC/FCY by mult_t_lap_fcy=1.4. Total race length tot_no_laps=71 for this circuit.
key_findings.numbers: standstill 1.9s (+0.43-1.37s team); inlap 2.691s; outlap 11.396s; ~20s normal pit loss vs ~10s under SC; SC lap multiplier 1.6, VSC/FCY 1.4

key_findings.claim: Heilmeier et al. (2020) 'Application of Monte Carlo Methods...' is THE paper for stochastic F1 strategy. It models accidents/failures, full-course-yellow & safety-car phases, driver start performance, and lap-time/pit-stop variability with empirical discrete distributions, and uses a 'ghost car' to inject SC dynamics realistically. Typical validation run count: 10,000 runs of a 20-car race.
key_findings.detail: Concrete empirical distributions (from pars_mcs.ini): probability of N safety-car phases in a race p_sc_quant=[0.455, 0.413, 0.099, 0.033] for N=0,1,2,3 (i.e. ~54.5% chance of at least one SC). SC duration distribution (laps 1-10) p_sc_duration=[0, 0.182, 0.25, 0.227, 0.193, 0.057, 0.068, 0.023, 0, 0] (mode ~3-4 laps). VSC duration p_vsc_duration=[0.479, 0.396, 0.021, 0.104] for 1-4 laps. SC start-timing distribution across race thirds p_sc_start=[0.364, 0.136, 0.136, 0.08, 0.193, 0.091]. P(VSC follows a retirement)=0.227. Team failure probabilities per race 0.041-0.225. Driver start-performance offsets mean -0.097..+0.102 s, sigma 0.098-0.245 s. Pit-stop duration sampled from team-specific Fisk (log-logistic) distributions (e.g. Mercedes shape/loc/scale = 1.563, -0.046, 0.48). NOTE: an official erratum to this paper exists (Appl. Sci. 2020, 10, 5745) - check it before copying numbers.
key_findings.numbers: 10,000 runs (20 cars); P(>=1 SC)=0.545; SC duration mode 3-4 laps; VSC 1-2 laps (87% of cases); P(VSC|failure)=0.227; team failure 4-22.5%; pit duration ~ Fisk/log-logistic

key_findings.claim: Exhaustive enumeration over stops/compounds is tractable and is the recommended baseline. The TUM optimizer loops over number of stops, then uses itertools to enumerate compound sequences, then (for a free track) places stop laps by solving/searching; because order of compounds doesn't change total free-track time, it uses combinations_with_replacement to prune.
key_findings.detail: Algorithm: for n_stops in [min_no_pitstops .. max_no_pitstops]: generate compound assignments for n_stops+1 stints via itertools.combinations_with_replacement(available_compounds, n_stops+1) (order-independent for free-track time) or itertools.product(...) if order matters; filter out single-compound strategies when enforce_diff_compounds=True (FIA rule: >=2 dry compounds must be used); keep only strategies containing the mandated starting compound if fixed. For each compound set, optimal stop laps on a free track minimize total time and can be found by a quadratic/convex optimization (degradation is convex) or by enumerating integer stop laps. State for full DP is (lap, current compound, tire age); Bellman recursion minimizes remaining race time. Real F1 races: typically 1-3 stops, 3 compounds -> only tens to low-hundreds of candidate strategies, so brute force over compound-sets x stop-laps is cheap.
key_findings.numbers: loop n_stops in [min..max]; stints = n_stops+1; combinations_with_replacement(compounds, n_stops+1); FIA rule >=2 dry compounds; practical 1-3 stops

key_findings.claim: Aguad & Thraves (2024, EJOR) formalize the competitive two-car problem as a zero-sum FEEDBACK STACKELBERG GAME solved by dynamic programming: each lap the leader chooses (stay/pit + compound) first, then the follower responds; both also pick a starting compound simultaneously pre-race. This is the rigorous game-theoretic upgrade to single-car DP.
key_findings.detail: State per car includes lap, tire compound, tire age, and gap/position; they report solving instances with 'hundreds of millions of states'. Findings: a strategic driver vs a non-strategic opponent raises win probability by >15%; win-probability-maximizing play is riskier than time-gap-minimizing play; yellow flags tend to benefit the trailing/underperforming driver (because cheap pit stops let them recover). Companion SSRN paper (Aguad & Thraves) frames the same as a zero-sum feedback Stackelberg game.
key_findings.numbers: two-player zero-sum Stackelberg DP; hundreds of millions of states; +15% win probability from strategic play; yellow flags favor trailing car

key_findings.claim: Robust vs expected-value optimization: because the time-optimal deterministic strategy is often NOT the most robust once safety cars are included, you should optimize a statistic of the OUTCOME DISTRIBUTION (e.g. expected finishing position, P(win), or a CVaR/worst-case tail), not just expected race time. Monte Carlo over the SC/failure distributions gives you that distribution.
key_findings.detail: Heilmeier et al. (2020) explicitly motivate Monte Carlo as a way to 'assess the ROBUSTNESS of race strategies' - run each candidate strategy through N stochastic races and compare the full distribution of finishing time/position, not a point estimate. Practical recipe: (1) enumerate candidate strategies (exhaustive), (2) for each, run N Monte Carlo races sampling SC/VSC/failures/noise, (3) score by E[position], P(podium/win), and a tail measure (e.g. 90th-percentile worst outcome / CVaR), (4) pick the strategy on the efficient frontier per risk appetite. Aguad & Thraves show the win-maximizing strategy is deliberately riskier (higher variance) than the gap-minimizing one - concrete evidence the objective choice changes the answer.
key_findings.numbers: score each strategy over N MC runs by E[pos], P(win), and CVaR/tail; robust optimum != deterministic time-optimum once SCs included

key_findings.claim: Reinforcement-learning approaches now exist and beat fixed baselines. Thomas et al. (2025) use a Deep Recurrent Q-Network (DRQN) for pit/compound decisions on top of Mercedes' Monte Carlo simulator and report finishing P5.33 vs P5.86 for the team SOTA. Heilmeier's repo also ships a DQN 'Virtual Strategy Engineer'.
key_findings.detail: Thomas et al. (2025) 'Explainable RL for F1 Race Strategy': DRQN; 24-feature state (track id, SC status {Full/Virtual/None}, position 1-20, race progress 0-1, current compound, deg/lap, tire-availability flags, gaps to leader/ahead/behind scaled to [-1,1], lap-time ratio); 4 actions/lap (no-pit, pit soft/medium/hard); reward +1 per lap survived, -10 per extra pit, -1000 invalid action, terminal = 100x F1 points (25 for P1). Hyperparams: lr=1e-3, gamma=0.99, replay buffer 1000 episodes, target update every 100, eps starts 1.0; ~1920 sims for testing, ~900/track for generalization; explainability via TimeSHAP (5% MAE) and VIPER decision-tree surrogate (92.6% acc). Heilmeier's VSE: two supervised NNs (pit-yes/no + compound choice) trained on 2014-2019 timing data, plus per-track DQN models. Newer arXiv work (2025-2026) adds Soft Actor-Critic for combined energy+tire strategy (8-dim state, ~4 h training) and multi-agent learning-based strategies.
key_findings.numbers: DRQN: 24-state, 4-action; reward +1/lap, -10 extra pit, -1000 invalid, terminal 100x points; lr 1e-3, gamma 0.99, buffer 1000, target/100, ~1920 train sims; result P5.33 vs SOTA P5.86

key_findings.claim: Real-time pit-wall re-optimization on a safety car: the strategist re-runs the simulation/optimizer live the moment an SC/VSC is declared, because the SC roughly halves pit loss (~20s -> ~10s) and flips undercut vs overcut economics. The decision reduces to comparing delta-time of pitting-now vs staying-out across the remaining-race distribution.
key_findings.detail: Operational pattern: strategy is decided lap-by-lap from live telemetry (tire temps, deg rate, gaps), not fixed pre-race. On SC deployment, re-evaluate by (a) recomputing pit loss with the SC multiplier (TUM: mult_t_lap_sc=1.6, so the in-lap/out-lap penalty shrinks because everyone is slow), (b) re-running the candidate-strategy Monte Carlo from the current state, (c) choosing the strategy maximizing expected position over the remaining laps. Undercut (pit early, exploit fresh-tire pace) loses value under SC since out-lap pace is capped; overcut/'pit under SC' gains value. Quantitatively: a normal stop costs ~20s of track position; under SC ~10s, often a 'free' stop. The undercut/overcut comparison is the fresh-tire out-lap delta vs the old-tire in-lap delta of the rival - a 1-2 lap delta-time lookup, the lightweight version of the full DP that fits the few-seconds decision window.
key_findings.numbers: pit loss ~20s normal -> ~10s under SC (~halved); SC lap multiplier 1.6; decision = remaining-race MC re-run / undercut-overcut delta-time within seconds

key_findings.claim: Foundational lineage: Bekker & Lotz (2009) built the first race simulation for strategy evaluation (discrete-event, validated on three 2005 races); Heine & Thraves (2023) and Aguad & Thraves (2024) add dynamic programming; Bonomi et al. (2023) use evolutionary algorithms; Duhr et al. (2023) add energy allocation. This chain is the canonical citation set.
key_findings.detail: Bekker, J. & Lotz, W. (2009) 'Planning Formula One race strategies using discrete-event simulation', J. Operational Research Society 60(7):952-961 - models car failures, passing, pit stops; time-based DES; validated on 3 races from 2005. Subsequent DP work (Heine & Thraves 2023; Aguad & Thraves 2024 EJOR) and evolutionary work (Bonomi et al. 2023) build on the same simulation-then-optimize idea. Heilmeier's 2022 TUM PhD thesis ('Simulation of circuit races for the objective evaluation of race strategy decisions') is the consolidated reference.
key_findings.numbers: Bekker & Lotz 2009 JORS 60(7):952-961, validated on 3 races from 2005 season

concrete_numbers: Monte Carlo run counts: TUM racesim default no_sim_runs=1 (deterministic); switch to MC at no_sim_runs>1; Heilmeier et al. (2020) validate with 10,000 runs of a 20-car race; industry articles cite 'thousands to millions' but ~10,000 is the standard for a converged outcome distribution
Lap time model: T_lap = t_q + t_gap_racepace + t_lap_sens_mass*fuel_mass + tire_deg(age,compound) + DRS + SC/FCY/pit corrections + N(0,sigma)
t_q (qualifying ref) = 63.003 s; t_gap_racepace = 4.036 s (Spielberg 2019)
Fuel: t_lap_sens_mass = 0.019 s/kg; b_fuel_perlap = 1.549 kg/lap; m_fuel start = 110 kg -> full tank ~2.1 s/lap decaying linearly to 0
Tire degradation (linear): t_tire = k_0 + k_1_lin*age; soft k_1~0.0232, medium ~0.0167, hard ~0.0100 s/lap; quadratic k_2 ~ 0.0001-0.0007 s/lap^2 (Spielberg 2019, Hamilton)
DRS effect = -0.322 s/lap
Pit stop: standstill t_pit_tirechange_min = 1.9 s (+0.43-1.37 s team); inlap loss 2.691 s; outlap loss 11.396 s; total free-track pit loss ~20 s; under SC ~10 s
Safety car / VSC lap-time multipliers: SC mult_t_lap_sc = 1.6; VSC/FCY mult_t_lap_fcy = 1.4
VSC duration (laps 1-4) = [0.479, 0.396, 0.021, 0.104]; P(VSC | retirement) = 0.227
Team failure probability per race = 0.041-0.225; driver lap-time noise sigma = 0.46-0.86 s; start-performance offset mean -0.097..+0.102 s, sigma 0.098-0.245 s
Pit-stop duration distribution: team-specific Fisk / log-logistic (e.g. Mercedes shape/loc/scale = 1.563, -0.046, 0.48)
Race length example tot_no_laps = 71 (Spielberg/Austria 2019)
Exhaustive search size: F1 practical 1-3 stops x 3 compounds -> tens to low-hundreds of candidate strategies; use itertools.combinations_with_replacement(compounds, n_stops+1)
DP state = (lap, current compound, tire age); Aguad-Thraves competitive DP solves 'hundreds of millions of states', gives >15% win-prob uplift

RL (DRQN, Thomas 2025): 24-feature state, 4 actions/lap; reward +1/lap, -10 extra pit, -1000 invalid, terminal 100x points; lr 1e-3, gamma 0.99, replay 1000 eps, target/100; result P5.33 vs SOTA P5.86
FIA rule to encode: >=2 distinct dry compounds must be used in a dry race (constrains compound enumeration)
findings.modelling_recommendation: Build it in three layers and reuse the open-source TUM FTM 'race-simulation' code (github.com/TUMFTM/race-simulation) as scaffolding. LAYER 1 - lap-discretized simulator: total race time = sum over laps of T_lap, where T_lap = base(t_q + race-pace gap) + 0.019*fuel_mass(lap) + tire_deg(age,compound) + DRS - and add pit loss on stop laps (~20s split into inlap 2.7s + standstill 1.9s + outlap 11.4s) and scale laps under SC by 1.6 / under VSC by 1.4. Model tire_deg as a per-compound polynomial in tire age; linear (k_0 + k_1*age) is the cheap default, quadratic if you have the data (soft k_1~0.023, med ~0.017, hard ~0.010 s/lap). Fuel mass = 110 - 1.549*lap kg. LAYER 2 - optimization: (a) DETERMINISTIC/free-track baseline by exhaustive enumeration - loop n_stops in 1..3, enumerate compound sequences with itertools.combinations_with_replacement(compounds, n_stops+1), enforce the FIA >=2-compound rule, and for each compound set place stop laps by integer search or a convex/quadratic solve (degradation is convex so optimum is unique); this is the racesim_basic approach and runs in milliseconds. (b) For the competitive/exact version, solve the DP over state=(lap, compound, tire_age) with a Bellman backward recursion minimizing remaining time; upgrade to Aguad-Thraves zero-sum feedback Stackelberg DP for two-car interaction (leader chooses, follower responds each lap). LAYER 3 - robustness via Monte Carlo: do NOT just pick the deterministic time-optimum. For each candidate strategy from Layer 2, run ~10,000 stochastic races sampling: number of SCs from [0.455,0.413,0.099,0.033], SC start lap and duration (mode 3-4 laps), VSC after failures (p=0.227, 1-2 laps), team failures (4-22.5%), per-lap Gaussian noise (sigma 0.46-0.86s), and Fisk-distributed pit durations. Score each strategy by the OUTCOME DISTRIBUTION - E[finishing position], P(win/podium), and a tail/CVaR measure - then choose on the risk-appetite frontier (win-maximizing is deliberately riskier/higher-variance than gap-minimizing). Use the 'ghost car' trick (Heilmeier 2020) to inject SC dynamics: run a virtual SC-paced car and clamp real cars to it during SC laps, which correctly bunches the field and halves effective pit loss. REAL-TIME PIT WALL: keep a fast (vectorized NumPy) version that, on SC declaration, re-runs the candidate-strategy Monte Carlo FROM THE CURRENT STATE (current lap, tire age, gaps) with the SC pit-loss (~10s) and SC lap multiplier active, and re-ranks; for the sub-second undercut/overcut call, fall back to a 1-2 lap delta-time comparison (fresh-tire out-lap delta vs rival old-tire in-lap delta). GOTCHAS: (1) check the official erratum to Heilmeier 2020 (Appl. Sci. 10, 5745) before copying distribution numbers; (2) the repo's cubic tire model has a known bug reusing quadratic coefficients - use lin/quad; (3) all the tire/lap coefficients above are circuit- and season-specific (Spielberg 2019) - refit per track from FastF1/free-practice data; (4) encode the FIA two-compound rule or your enumerator will return illegal strategies.

findings.topic: Surrogate modelling and data fusion for accelerating expensive simulators, applied to real-time F1 strategy (instant emulation + live Bayesian tyre-deg re-estimation)

key_findings.claim: A surrogate (emulator/meta-model) approximates an expensive simulator from a modest set of input-output pairs, then evaluates in milliseconds instead of hours; typical architectures are Gaussian process regression (kriging), neural networks, and tree ensembles (XGBoost), each trading accuracy/interpretability/cost.
key_findings.detail: Surrogate replaces the simulator inside optimization, sensitivity, and uncertainty-quantification loops. Empirical comparisons find ANNs and gradient-boosted trees often outperform GP/kriging surrogates on accuracy AND compute, with XGBoost frequently the strongest on precision and efficiency; GPs remain valuable for their built-in uncertainty (predictive variance). For a Monte Carlo F1 race sim, you want a regressor mapping {strategy params, lap, tyre age, compound, traffic/gap, track state} -> {predicted lap time / finishing position / outcome distribution}.
key_findings.numbers: GP/kriging vs ML: XGBoost reported more precise + more compute-efficient than kriging in benchmark UQ studies (qualitative ranking, no single universal % given)

key_findings.claim: Surrogates enable real-time / latency-sensitive deployment by collapsing simulator runtime from hours to sub-millisecond–second inference, i.e. 3–6 orders of magnitude speedup.
key_findings.detail: This is the core enabler for in-race use: instead of running a fresh Monte Carlo race sim (seconds to minutes) for every candidate pit-window, a trained NN surrogate returns predictions essentially instantly, so thousands of strategy permutations can be scored per pit decision. The CFD literature gives the clearest hard numbers, and the same principle transfers to race sims.
key_findings.numbers: Neural-field aero surrogate: <0.1 s inference vs ~19 h CFD = ~6 orders of magnitude speedup; another model: 0.0012 s inference = ~100,000x speedup online; component breakdown ~80 ms geometry encoding + ~8 ms field prediction; neural operators: <1 s = >3 orders of magnitude

key_findings.claim: Multi-fidelity data fusion combines a cheap low-fidelity model with sparse high-fidelity data via the Kennedy-O'Hagan autoregressive co-kriging model: f_H(x) = rho * f_L(x) + delta(x).
key_findings.detail: rho is a scalar capturing the proportional relationship between low- and high-fidelity functions; delta(x) is an independent GP discrepancy term for systematic differences. The joint covariance is K = [[k_LL, rho*k_LL],[rho*k_LL, rho^2*k_LL + k_dd]]. Emukit implements both linear (this AR1) and non-linear (NARGP) versions in Python. For F1: low-fidelity = fast analytical/deterministic lap model or coarse sim; high-fidelity = full stochastic Monte Carlo sim or real telemetry; fuse to get cheap-but-accurate predictions.
key_findings.numbers: Reported case: multi-fidelity GP reached MSE 15.62 degC^2 using only 6% of possible high-fidelity simulations, vs >94 degC^2 for single-fidelity GP; general rule-of-thumb ~an order of magnitude fewer high-fidelity simulator calls

key_findings.claim: Online Bayesian linear regression IS a Kalman filter: regression weights theta are the hidden state, the covariate vector x_t^T is the (time-varying) observation matrix H_t, observation noise R = sigma^2; this gives exact recursive-least-squares / Bayesian-LR posterior updates in O(m^2) per step.
key_findings.detail: LG-SSM form: z_t ~ N(F z_{t-1}, Q), y_t ~ N(H_t z_t, R) with F=I, Q=0 (static weights) or Q>0 (slowly drifting weights — exactly what you want for tyre-deg coefficients that change as track rubbers in / temperature shifts). Setting Q>0 makes the filter adaptively forget old laps. This is directly implementable for a live tyre-deg updater: model lap_time = a + b*tyre_age (+ fuel term), put [a,b] in the state, update [a,b]'s Gaussian posterior every completed lap, set Q to control how fast deg estimate adapts.
key_findings.numbers: Update cost O(m^2) per observation, m = number of regression weights (here ~2-4); exact one-pass posterior; prior example Sigma0 = 10*I, F=I, Q=0

key_findings.claim: A Bayesian state-space framework for F1 tyre degradation has been published (Dec 2025), modelling lap time as baseline pace + fuel effect + latent tyre-degradation random walk, with pit stops as state resets, fit on free FastF1 timing data.
key_findings.detail: Observation: lap_time = baseline + fuel_effect + tyre_deg_effect; state transition: tyre wear as a random walk (latent pace accumulating per lap); pit stop resets the degradation state to a fresh-compound baseline and updates fuel mass deterministically. Extensions: compound-specific deg rates, time-varying deg, skewed-t observation model for asymmetric driver errors. Beats an ARIMA(2,1,2) baseline. Case study: Hamilton, 2025 Austrian GP. NOTE: this paper uses Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (Stan), i.e. batch MCMC, not a live filter — but the random-walk state-space structure is exactly what a Kalman/particle filter implements recursively for true real-time use.
key_findings.numbers: Fuel coefficient reported by PDF summarizer as 0.107 s/kg (LOW CONFIDENCE — see flag; standard F1 value is ~0.03-0.04 s/kg); deg rate ~0.08-0.12 s/lap; MAE ~0.3-0.4 s/lap; ~15-22% RMSE reduction vs ARIMA (these numbers were summarizer-extracted from the PDF, not directly verified)

key_findings.claim: Standard F1 fuel-weight effect is roughly 0.03-0.04 seconds per lap per kg of fuel (~0.25-0.40 s per 10 kg), so this term is a known, near-linear correction to bake into the lap-time/surrogate model.
key_findings.detail: Use this to fuel-correct laps before estimating tyre deg, otherwise the falling fuel mass (car getting lighter ~1.5-2 kg/lap) masks/biases the deg signal. This is why the F1 tyre paper splits lap time into an explicit deterministic fuel term plus the latent deg state. The 0.107 s/kg figure my PDF summarizer reported for arXiv:2512.00640 is ~3x the well-established value, so treat it as a likely extraction error.
key_findings.numbers: 0.03 s/kg typical (range 0.025-0.040 s/kg); Prost F1 Catalunya 2001 sim: 0.32 s per 10 kg; ~0.035 s/kg cited historically

key_findings.claim: Particle filters (sequential Monte Carlo) are the right tool when the tyre-deg / race state model is nonlinear or non-Gaussian (e.g. multi-modal: safety-car vs green, or a skewed-t error model), generalizing the Kalman filter at higher compute cost.
key_findings.detail: PF approximates the posterior with N weighted particles; handles nonlinearity/multimodality the (extended) Kalman filter cannot, but compute scales with N and real-time performance is a design constraint (degeneracy, resampling, importance density choice). For F1: a few hundred to a few thousand particles is typically tractable per lap. Use Kalman/Bayesian-LR if you keep the deg model linear-Gaussian (cheapest, exact); upgrade to PF only if you add the skewed-t / regime-switching (SC) structure.
key_findings.numbers: N particles drives cost/accuracy; hundreds-to-thousands feasible online on modern hardware; EKF cheaper but biased for strong nonlinearity

key_findings.claim: A neural-network surrogate trained on a Monte Carlo F1 race simulator is an established, published approach for real-time strategy optimization (and ANN+MCTS is the canonical Formula-E precedent).
key_findings.detail: arXiv:2512.21570 (Dec 2025) trains a neural surrogate on Monte Carlo race-sim outputs to avoid repeated expensive simulation calls during inference, enabling near-instant strategy evaluation in-race (no clean per-number benchmark extractable from the PDF). The Formula-E paper (Springer NCA 2020) combines ANNs with Monte Carlo Tree Search for race-strategy development, and the 'Virtual Strategy Engineer' (MDPI Applied Sciences 2020) uses ANNs for circuit-motorsport strategy decisions. Together these establish the exact pattern requested: MC sim -> NN surrogate -> fast strategy search.
key_findings.numbers: No clean per-number benchmarks legibly extractable from arXiv:2512.21570 PDF; relationship is qualitative (near-instant vs per-strategy MC runs)

key_findings.claim: A purely data-driven Bi-LSTM pit-stop classifier on FastF1 telemetry gives strong real-world numbers, useful as a benchmark / complement to a physics-based surrogate.
key_findings.detail: 3 stacked Bi-LSTM layers (256/128/64 units) + dense sigmoid, 10-timestep windows, 10 telemetry features (lap time, position, compound, tyre life, track status, whether car ahead/behind pitted, etc.). Trained on 2020-2024 seasons. Not framed as a simulator surrogate (it's a classifier), but demonstrates achievable in-race predictive accuracy from the same free FastF1 data you'd use to train a surrogate / drive a live filter.
key_findings.numbers: 99,928 laps; pit-stop minority class 3.5% (3,131 pits); after SMOTE 88,299/class; test F1=0.81, precision=0.77, recall=0.86, ROC-AUC=0.988, balanced acc=0.93; 2025 Chinese GP live: acc 70.6%, recall 92.3%, F1 0.80; Adam lr=5e-4, batch 32, 50 epochs

concrete_numbers: Surrogate inference speedup: 3-6 orders of magnitude vs simulator (e.g. <0.1 s vs ~19 h CFD; 0.0012 s = ~100,000x) [arxiv 2505.14704]
Surrogate inference latency: ~8 ms field prediction (+~80 ms geometry encoding) — well within an in-race per-lap (~90 s) or per-decision budget
Multi-fidelity AR1 / co-kriging: f_H(x) = rho*f_L(x) + delta(x); joint cov K=[[k_LL, rho*k_LL],[rho*k_LL, rho^2*k_LL+k_dd]]
Multi-fidelity efficiency: MSE 15.62 degC^2 using only 6% of high-fidelity sims vs >94 degC^2 single-fidelity; ~1 order of magnitude fewer HF calls
Kalman-as-Bayesian-LR: state=weights theta, F=I, Q=0 (static) or Q>0 (drifting deg), H_t=x_t^T, R=sigma^2; cost O(m^2)/lap, exact RLS posterior
F1 fuel effect: ~0.03-0.04 s/lap/kg (range 0.025-0.040); ~0.25-0.40 s per 10 kg; fuel burn ~1.5-2 kg/lap — fuel-correct before estimating deg
Tyre-deg model (F1 state-space, arxiv 2512.00640): lap_time = baseline + fuel_effect + tyre_deg(random walk); pit = state reset to fresh-compound baseline
Tyre-deg magnitude (medium-conf, summarizer-extracted): ~0.08-0.12 s/lap deg rate; MAE ~0.3-0.4 s/lap; ~15-22% RMSE reduction vs ARIMA(2,1,2)
Particle filter: N=hundreds-to-thousands of particles feasible online; use when adding nonlinear/multimodal (safety-car regime, skewed-t errors) structure
Bi-LSTM pit classifier benchmark: F1=0.81, recall=0.86, ROC-AUC=0.988 on 99,928 FastF1 laps (2020-2024); minority pit class only 3.5%
Data source for all F1 work: FastF1 Python API (free, public timing/telemetry) — same data trains the surrogate AND drives the live filter
findings.modelling_recommendation:
Two complementary components.

(A) PyTorch MLP surrogate of the Monte Carlo race sim. Run the MC sim offline to generate training data: sample inputs X = {pit lap(s), start compound, stint compounds, starting fuel, track state, gap to rivals, SC probability, lap index, tyre age} and labels Y = {predicted lap time OR final finishing position/Delta OR the outcome distribution's mean+variance}. Architecture: a 3-5 hidden-layer MLP (e.g. 256-128-64, ReLU, dropout ~0.2), Adam lr~5e-4, MSE loss for regression; normalize inputs. To preserve the MC sim's stochasticity, either (i) predict mean and log-variance (heteroscedastic Gaussian NLL loss) so you keep an uncertainty estimate, or (ii) train an ensemble of 5 MLPs and use spread as uncertainty. This gives ~ms inference, so you can score thousands of strategy permutations per pit decision instead of re-running the sim. If you have a cheap analytical lap model too, wrap it as low-fidelity and use multi-fidelity fusion (Emukit linear/NARGP, or just feed the LF prediction as an extra MLP input) to cut required MC runs ~10x — implement the Kennedy-O'Hagan AR1 form f_H = rho*f_L + delta. Gotcha: GP surrogates give uncertainty for free but scale O(n^3) and are weaker than NN/XGBoost on accuracy+speed in benchmarks; prefer MLP or XGBoost for the main surrogate, reserve GP/co-kriging for the data-fusion layer where uncertainty and few HF points matter.

(B) Kalman / Bayesian live tyre-deg updater. Model each stint's pace as lap_time_corrected = a + b*tyre_age, where lap_time_corrected = raw_lap_time - fuel_effect (fuel_effect = 0.03 s/kg * remaining_fuel_kg; subtract this first using a known burn rate ~1.6 kg/lap). Put the state z=[a,b] (intercept = fresh-tyre pace, slope = deg rate s/lap) into a Kalman filter: F=I, H_t=[1, tyre_age_t], R=sigma_lap^2 (lap-time noise, ~0.1-0.3 s^2), and crucially Q=small diagonal>0 so the deg estimate adapts as the track evolves (rubber-in, temperature, clouds). This is exactly recursive Bayesian linear regression — exact O(m^2) Gaussian posterior update every completed lap, giving a live [a,b] mean+covariance you can extrapolate to forecast remaining-stint pace and the optimal pit lap. At a pit stop, reset the state (re-inflate covariance / reset to a fresh-compound prior) — the state-reset trick from arXiv:2512.00640. Tune Q by how fast you want to trust new laps vs history. Upgrade path: if you want compound-specific behavior, multi-modal safety-car regimes, or the published skewed-t error model, swap the Kalman filter for a particle filter (a few hundred-thousand particles, still real-time) — same state, nonlinear/non-Gaussian capable. Validate against FastF1 historical races. Honest caveats: the specific F1 deg/fuel numbers from arXiv:2512.00640 came via a PDF auto-summarizer and the 0.107 s/kg fuel figure is ~3x the well-established ~0.03 s/kg, so treat that paper's exact constants as unverified and re-derive coefficients by fitting FastF1 data yourself; the paper itself uses batch HMC/Stan, so the real-time recursive filter is your adaptation, not their published method.

findings.topic: Public data sources & APIs for calibrating an F1 strategy / tyre-degradation model on real race data in Python (FastF1 + Jolpica-Ergast)

key_findings.claim: FastF1 is the primary Python library for per-lap, stint, compound, tyre-life, track-status and telemetry data; session.laps returns a pandas-DataFrame subclass (Laps) with all the columns needed for tyre-degradation calibration.
key_findings.detail: Workflow: import fastf1; fastf1.Cache.enable_cache('~/fastf1_cache'); session = fastf1.get_session(2024, 'Bahrain', 'R'); session.load(); laps = session.laps. session.load() pulls laps, telemetry, weather and race-control messages from F1's live timing APIs. laps is a Laps object (subclass of pandas.DataFrame). Key tyre-degradation columns: LapTime (timedelta), LapNumber (int), Stint (int), Compound (SOFT/MEDIUM/HARD/INTERMEDIATE/WET/UNKNOWN), TyreLife (laps on current tyre incl. laps before data start), FreshTyre (bool, new tyre at stint start), PitInTime / PitOutTime (session-time timedeltas), TrackStatus (string of concatenated status codes that occurred during the lap), IsAccurate (bool, passed validation - critical filter for degradation work), Deleted / DeletedReason, Sector1/2/3Time, SpeedI1/I2/FL/ST (km/h), Driver, Team, Position. Useful Laps methods: pick_drivers(), pick_quicklaps(threshold default 1.07 i.e. 107% of fastest), pick_compounds(), pick_track_status(status, how='equals'|'contains'|'excludes'|'any'|'none'), pick_wo_box() (drop in/out laps), pick_box_laps(), pick_fastest().
key_findings.numbers: pick_quicklaps default threshold 1.07 (107%); weather_data sampled ~1/minute; Compound enum: SOFT, MEDIUM, HARD, INTERMEDIATE, WET, UNKNOWN, TEST_UNKNOWN

key_findings.claim: FastF1's underlying data source is the official F1 live-timing service (with schedule/results backfilled from the Ergast/Jolpica API); caching is built in and strongly recommended.
key_findings.detail: All API requests are cached locally once you call fastf1.Cache.enable_cache(path). Caching should almost always be enabled to speed up scripts and to avoid hitting upstream rate limits. The session timing/telemetry data comes from F1's live timing API; non-live metadata (event schedule, classification) can come from the Ergast-compatible backend (now Jolpica). The F1ApiSupport / Ergast-availability is exposed on the event schedule. Cache is a simple on-disk folder; once populated, re-runs do not re-download.
key_findings.numbers: Cache call: fastf1.Cache.enable_cache('/path/to/cache')

key_findings.claim: Jolpica-Ergast (api.jolpi.ca) is the drop-in, backwards-compatible successor to the shut-down ergast.com API; base URL is http://api.jolpi.ca/ergast/f1/ and it serves results, laps, pitstops, qualifying, standings, etc.
key_findings.detail: Endpoints (each must end with '/' or '.json'): /ergast/f1/circuits/, /ergast/f1/drivers/, /ergast/f1/constructors/, /ergast/f1/{season}/{round}/results/, /ergast/f1/{season}/{round}/laps/, /ergast/f1/{season}/{round}/pitstops/, /ergast/f1/{season}/qualifying/, /ergast/f1/{season}/driverstandings/, /ergast/f1/{season}/constructorstandings/, /ergast/f1/{season}/sprint/, /ergast/f1/status/, /ergast/f1/seasons/. For gaps, the original Ergast docs at ergast.com/mrd/ still apply. Ergast's own ergast.com endpoint was deprecated at end of 2024.
key_findings.numbers: Base: http://api.jolpi.ca/ergast/f1/

key_findings.claim: The Jolpica laps endpoint gives per-lap times per driver; the pitstops endpoint gives pit-stop DURATION in seconds plus lap and clock time.
key_findings.detail: Laps: GET http://api.jolpi.ca/ergast/f1/{season}/{round}/laps/ -> MRData.RaceTable.Races[0].Laps, each Lap has number and a Timings array of {driverId, position, time} where time is the lap time as 'm:ss.sss' (e.g. '1:37.284'). You can filter to one driver: /{season}/{round}/drivers/{driverId}/laps/ and one lap: /{season}/{round}/laps/{lapNumber}/. Pitstops: GET http://api.jolpi.ca/ergast/f1/{season}/{round}/pitstops/ -> each PitStop has {driverId, lap, stop, time (HH:mm:ss clock), duration}. duration is the stationary+lane time in seconds as a string, e.g. '20.006', and per the docs 'including pit entry, exit and red flag time, if necessary'. Verified live: 2024 Bahrain (round 1) laps endpoint returns MRData total=1129 lap-records, e.g. {driverId:'max_verstappen', position:'1', time:'1:37.284'}.
key_findings.numbers: Example pit-stop duration field: "20.006" (seconds). Example lap time: "1:37.284". 2024 Bahrain laps total=1129 records.

key_findings.claim: Jolpica rate limits are strict: 4 requests/second burst and 500 requests/hour sustained (unauthenticated); exceeding returns HTTP 429.
key_findings.detail: Maintainer-stated limits: burst 4 req/s, sustained 500 req/hour for unauthenticated use; the maintainer warns this may DECREASE once self-service API tokens exist, and a lower ~200 req/hour figure has also been quoted as a load-adjusted floor. No built-in retry; recommended mitigation is to reduce call volume via filtering, request a token for higher limits, and add your own client-side backoff. Because laps are paginated at max 100 records/page, a full race's lap data (1000+ records) needs many requests - so cache aggressively. FastF1 with caching is the better path for bulk per-lap timing; use Jolpica directly mainly for pit-stop durations and results which FastF1 does not expose as cleanly.
key_findings.numbers: Burst 4 req/s; sustained 500 req/hour (some sources: 200/hour load-adjusted); pagination limit default 30, MAX 100, offset default 0; 429 on exceed

key_findings.claim: FastF1 TrackStatus integer codes let you flag safety-car / VSC / red-flag laps to exclude them from degradation fitting.
key_findings.detail: Single-digit string codes (can be concatenated within one lap's TrackStatus): '1' = track clear/green; '2' = yellow flag; '4' = Safety Car; '5' = Red Flag; '6' = Virtual Safety Car deployed; '7' = VSC ending (actual end marked by a return to '1'). Code '3' has never been observed. For clean tyre-deg data, filter laps.pick_track_status('1', how='equals') (green-only) and laps.pick_wo_box(), then optionally pick_quicklaps().
key_findings.numbers: Codes: 1 green, 2 yellow, 4 SC, 5 red, 6 VSC deployed, 7 VSC ending; 3 unused

concrete_numbers: FastF1 install: pip install fastf1 (current series 3.8.x)
Enable cache: fastf1.Cache.enable_cache('~/fastf1_cache')
Load session: fastf1.get_session(2024, 'Bahrain', 'R').load()
pick_quicklaps default threshold = 1.07 (107% of fastest lap)
Jolpica base URL: http://api.jolpi.ca/ergast/f1/
Jolpica rate limit: 4 requests/second burst, 500 requests/hour sustained (unauth); HTTP 429 on breach
Jolpica pagination: limit default 30, MAX 100, offset default 0
Laps endpoint: http://api.jolpi.ca/ergast/f1/{season}/{round}/laps/ (Timings[] = {driverId, position, time})
Pitstops endpoint: http://api.jolpi.ca/ergast/f1/{season}/{round}/pitstops/ (duration in seconds, e.g. '20.006')
Per-driver laps: http://api.jolpi.ca/ergast/f1/{season}/{round}/drivers/{driverId}/laps/
2024 Bahrain GP (round 1) laps endpoint: MRData total = 1129 lap records
Example lap time format: '1:37.284' (m:ss.sss); pit clock time format: HH:mm:ss

Weather sampling: ~once per minute (AirTemp, TrackTemp, Humidity, Pressure, Rainfall, WindSpeed, WindDirection)
findings.modelling_recommendation:
Use FastF1 as the primary data source for tyre-degradation calibration and Jolpica-Ergast only for pit-stop durations and official results that FastF1 doesn't surface cleanly.

Data pipeline (Python):
1. import fastf1; fastf1.Cache.enable_cache('cache_dir') ONCE at startup (mandatory for speed + rate-limit safety).
2. session = fastf1.get_session(year, gp, 'R'); session.load(); laps = session.laps.
3. Build a clean degradation dataset: clean = laps.pick_wo_box().pick_track_status('1', how='equals').pick_quicklaps(1.07). This drops in/out laps, non-green (SC/VSC/red/yellow) laps, and outliers. Keep also IsAccurate==True.
4. Convert LapTime/PitInTime/PitOutTime from pandas Timedelta to seconds via .dt.total_seconds().

Degradation model: group clean laps by (Driver, Stint, Compound). Within each stint, regress LapTime_seconds on TyreLife (use TyreLife not just lap-in-stint count, because it accounts for laps run before the data window and reflects true tyre age). A simple per-compound model is: lap_time = base_pace(compound) + fuel_correction*(laps_remaining) + deg_rate(compound)*TyreLife, where deg_rate is the slope (s/lap) you calibrate. Fuel effect (~0.03-0.06 s/lap per lap of fuel burned) is roughly linear and must be removed/co-fitted before attributing the residual slope to tyre wear, otherwise fuel-burn-off masks/offsets degradation. Fit base_pace and deg_rate per compound; allow a small quadratic TyreLife^2 term for cliff behaviour on softer compounds.

Stint/pit modelling: for each Stint, the boundary is where Compound changes or PitInTime/PitOutTime are non-null. Get the actual pit-loss time from Jolpica pitstops endpoint (duration field, seconds) and add a track-specific pit-lane delta (entry+exit travel time, ~18-25 s total time-lost depending on circuit; the Jolpica duration already says it includes entry/exit). Use this as the strategy model's pit penalty.

Gotchas: (a) TrackStatus on a lap is a CONCATENATION of all statuses seen that lap, so use how='contains'/'excludes' to catch partial-SC laps, not just exact match. (b) FastF1 timedeltas need .total_seconds(). (c) FastF1 telemetry/weather download is slow on first run — cache. (d) Jolpica laps are paginated at max 100/page and a race has 1000+ records, so prefer FastF1 for bulk per-lap timing and reserve Jolpica calls (with client-side backoff and ETag/local caching) for pit durations and results to stay under 4 req/s & 500 req/hr. (e) Compound values may be 'UNKNOWN' for some sessions/years — filter those out. (f) Jolpica has had reported lap-time data-correction issues for some 2024 races vs Ergast, so cross-check FastF1 lap times (from F1 live timing) against Jolpica when accuracy matters.

findings.topic: F1 race-strategy software landscape and what would "shock" a Williams Racing strategy team reviewing a portfolio for the "Senior AI and Modelling Engineer - Strategy" role (Grove, UK)

key_findings.claim: The Williams 'Senior AI and Modelling Engineer - Strategy' role sits in the Technology & Innovation Group and explicitly wants PyTorch/Scikit-learn ML applied to race strategy, simulation, data fusion, predictive analytics, anomaly detection and optimisation - a portfolio should speak that exact stack.
key_findings.detail: Williams careers postings for the strategy/AI roles call for: 'design and train AI models for vehicle dynamics, race strategy, and operational efficiency', 'build machine learning pipelines for simulation, data fusion, and predictive analytics', 'develop anomaly detection and optimisation models', delivering insights 'using state-of-the-art frameworks like PyTorch and Scikit-learn'. The Senior AI Engineer sibling role adds deep/reinforcement learning, 'scalable ML pipelines for real-time simulation', 'model interpretability and explainable AI', LLMs/transformers, Python + C++. The Head of Data & AI role is building/scaling a defined data platform and a team of data scientists. Match your portfolio's language and stack to these.
key_findings.numbers: Frameworks named: Python, PyTorch, TensorFlow, Scikit-learn; C++ beneficial. Role family: Technology & Innovation Group, Grove/Wantage UK.

key_findings.claim: Williams' publicly-known modern tech direction is the Atlassian title partnership (Feb 2025) - 'System of Work', data consolidation and GenAI - NOT a public race-strategy simulator. The strategy engine itself is in-house and opaque, which is exactly the gap a strong portfolio can speak to.
key_findings.detail: Atlassian became Official Title + Technology Partner in Feb 2025 (described as the biggest deal in Williams' ~48-year history). Williams had 23 different tracking systems and is consolidating onto Jira Service Management, Confluence, Assets, plus Rovo (Atlassian's GenAI) for auto-reports and agent-surfaced insights. This shows a team actively modernising off spreadsheets/scattered tools - a candidate who builds clean, productionised, well-documented tooling fits the cultural moment. Results context: Williams scored 84 points total across 2018-2024 but 111 points in 2025 alone, signalling momentum and investment.
key_findings.numbers: Atlassian deal Feb 2025; 23 tracking systems being consolidated; Williams 84 pts (2018-2024 combined) vs 111 pts in 2025 alone.

key_findings.claim: The famous 'AWS powers F1' story is mostly about Formula 1 the championship/broadcast (F1 Insights, Track Pulse, IT support), not teams' pit-wall strategy engines. Do NOT assume Williams' strategy stack is AWS - that distinction itself signals you understand the landscape.
key_findings.detail: AWS is F1's (FOM's) official cloud/ML provider since 2018: ~300 sensors/car, >1 million data points/second, SageMaker for F1 Insights broadcast graphics, EC2 HPC cutting CFD/aero sim times 70% (helped 2022 car cut wake downforce loss from 50% to 15%), Bedrock GenAI cutting race-day IT issue resolution 86%. These are broadcast/FOM/regulatory CFD use cases. Individual teams choose their own clouds and keep strategy software proprietary; there is no public confirmation Williams' strategy simulator runs on AWS. Treat cloud-for-strategy as low confidence.
key_findings.numbers: ~300 sensors/car; >1M data points/sec; CFD sim time cut 70%; wake downforce loss 50%->15% (2022 car); 86% faster IT resolution via Bedrock; AWS-F1 partnership since 2018.

key_findings.claim: The de-facto industry pit-wall tool is Catapult RaceWatch (origin McLaren/Honda 2008, credited across ~20 world championships). The core method everywhere is Monte Carlo race simulation producing 3-4 baseline strategies, continuously re-adapted. A portfolio that out-thinks RaceWatch's known weaknesses (speed, uncertainty, explainability) is what impresses.
key_findings.detail: RaceWatch ingests ~200 channels of video/audio/data and offers ~300 visualisations in role-specific dashboards; models base lap time, tyre degradation, pit loss, per-corner overtake probability, driver-specific mistake/overtake variance, safety-car impact, fuel. Teams run large Monte Carlo batches to pre-compute 3-4 baseline strategies, then re-optimise live against actual degradation and rival pit calls (undercut/overcut). Monte Carlo strategy was pioneered by Neil Martin at McLaren in the 1990s. This is mature and ubiquitous - so novelty must come from HOW (speed, robustness, UQ, explainability), not WHAT.
key_findings.numbers: RaceWatch: ~200 data channels, ~300 visualisations; teams pre-compute 3-4 baseline strategies; Monte Carlo pioneered ~1990s (Neil Martin, McLaren); pit-wall decisions taken in seconds.

key_findings.claim: The single most credible 'shock' piece is an instant surrogate that replaces a Monte Carlo batch with a sub-second what-if engine. State-space tyre models already take 15-30s to run; a neural/GP surrogate giving full-race strategy distributions in <1s on the pit wall is a genuine, demonstrable edge.
key_findings.detail: A Bayesian state-space tyre-degradation model (arXiv 2512.00640, Dec 2025) takes 15-30 seconds per run - usable within a lap but too slow for sweeping thousands of what-ifs interactively. Classic Monte Carlo strategy needs large batches per decision. A portfolio that trains a fast surrogate (e.g. neural net / Gaussian process) on a calibrated Monte Carlo simulator, then serves full strategy-space evaluation (every pit-lap x compound combination with win/position probability) in <1 second, directly attacks the latency pain a real pit wall feels when a safety car drops with seconds to decide. Pair it with a clean what-if UI.
key_findings.numbers: Bayesian state-space tyre model runtime: 15-30 s/run (arXiv 2512.00640). Target to 'shock': interactive full-strategy-space what-if in <1 s. Pit-wall decision budget: seconds.

key_findings.claim: Live Bayesian tyre updating with explicit uncertainty bands is a published, beatable benchmark - and is exactly what deep-learning approaches lack. Hitting/beating ~1.08s RMSPE per stint with calibrated uncertainty, updating live each lap, is concrete and impressive.
key_findings.detail: The Bayesian state-space tyre paper models lap time = f(fuel mass) + latent tyre pace, with pit stops as state resets, giving human-readable degradation rates (~0.054 s/lap) AND 90% credible intervals (~+/-0.15 s/lap). Reported skewed-t model RMSPE 1.082 s vs ARIMA 1.520 s across three stints; CRPS 0.202 vs 0.324; live lap-44 prediction from data through lap 43. The authors explicitly argue prior deep-learning tyre work 'lack[s] interpretability and explicit uncertainty quantification - features that are crucial in operational race environments'. A portfolio that does live Bayesian updating with calibrated bands, benchmarked against these published numbers, signals you understand operational UQ, not just point prediction.
key_findings.numbers: RMSPE: 1.082 s (skewed-t Bayesian) vs 1.169 s (base) vs 1.520 s (ARIMA), 3 stints; CRPS 0.202 vs 0.324; degradation ~0.054 s/lap; 90% credible interval ~+/-0.15 s; live lap-by-lap update.

key_findings.claim: Explainable strategy recommendation is an active, publishable but immature frontier - and Williams' own job spec demands 'model interpretability and explainable AI'. An RL/optimiser that outputs a recommendation PLUS a strategist-readable reason and counterfactual is directly on-brief.
key_findings.detail: RSRL (Race Strategy Reinforcement Learning, arXiv 2501.04068, Jan 2025) controls strategy in simulation and beat baselines on a 2023 Bahrain GP test (avg finish P5.33 vs best baseline P5.63, vs P5.5 expected pace) while adding explainability via feature importance, decision-tree surrogate models, and decision-tree counterfactuals to build strategist trust. Companion work (arXiv 2501.04067) forecasts 'tyre energy' from Mercedes-AMG PETRONAS historic telemetry using deep learning + XGBoost with feature-importance and counterfactual explanations. The margins are thin (tenths of a position) and explainability is bolted on, not native - so a portfolio with a natively explainable recommender (why-this-lap, what-if-not, confidence) is both novel and exactly what the role's 'explainable AI for strategists' wording asks for.
key_findings.numbers: RSRL avg finish P5.33 vs best baseline P5.63 (2023 Bahrain GP sim), pace baseline P5.5; explainability via feature importance + decision-tree surrogates + counterfactuals; companion paper uses real Mercedes-AMG PETRONAS telemetry.

key_findings.claim: Robust strategy under safety-car uncertainty is where races are won/lost and where naive optimisers fail. Demonstrating strategies optimised for the FULL distribution of SC outcomes (not the expected case), with 'ghost-car' SC modelling, would land hard.
key_findings.detail: Academic consensus (TUMFTM Heilmeier et al.) is that races are decided by random accidents/safety cars and that probabilistic effects must be modelled to find ROBUST strategies, using Monte Carlo with customised SC probability distributions and 'ghost car' approaches to test robustness. TUMFTM's open simulator covers tyre deg, fuel mass loss, pit loss, multi-car interactions and probabilistic SC/VSC, with parameter files auto-generated from a timing DB for 121 F1 races (2014-2019 seasons), in Python (cvxpy, quadprog). A portfolio that explicitly optimises for robustness (e.g. maximise expected position OR a risk-adjusted/CVaR objective across SC scenarios) and visualises the regret of the 'expected-case-optimal' plan when a SC actually hits would show genuine strategic maturity.
key_findings.numbers: TUMFTM simulator: 121 F1 races (2014-2019), Python 3.8 (cvxpy/cython/quadprog), lap-wise discretisation, Monte Carlo SC/VSC + 'ghost car'; models fuel mass loss, tyre deg, pit loss, interactions.

key_findings.claim: Public/academic models openly admit they are crippled by having only public timing data vs teams' proprietary sensor streams. The 'shock' is a candidate who builds a calibration harness that closes that gap on whatever data is available and quantifies the residual - showing you'd plug straight into real telemetry on day one.
key_findings.detail: A Bi-LSTM pit-stop predictor (Frontiers, 2025) hit precision 0.77 / recall 0.86 / F1 0.81 / balanced accuracy 0.93 on 99,928 laps (2020-2024), and 70.59% accuracy on the live 2025 Chinese GP - while explicitly conceding teams 'have access to proprietary data streams from hundreds of sensors' that the public-data model cannot match. A portfolio that (a) calibrates a simulator against real lap-time data, (b) reports calibration error honestly (e.g. RMSPE per stint), and (c) is architected so swapping public for proprietary telemetry only improves it, demonstrates the exact production-data mindset the role needs.
key_findings.numbers: Bi-LSTM pit predictor: precision 0.77, recall 0.86, F1 0.81, balanced accuracy 0.93 on 99,928 laps (2020-2024); 70.59% accuracy live 2025 Chinese GP; teams have 'hundreds of sensors' vs public data.

findings.modelling_recommendation: Build ONE cohesive portfolio piece - a 'live strategy co-pilot' - that stacks four things F1 teams individually struggle with, then benchmark each against published numbers so claims are verifiable. (1) CALIBRATED SIMULATOR: fork/rebuild a lap-wise Monte Carlo race sim (use TUMFTM as reference architecture: lap-time = base_pace + fuel_mass_effect(decreasing) + tyre_deg(compound) + traffic; pit loss ~20-24s green / much less under SC; per-corner overtake probabilities). Calibrate on public timing data (FastF1) and REPORT residual error honestly per stint (target RMSPE in the ~1.0-1.5 s range to match the state-space/ARIMA literature). (2) LIVE BAYESIAN TYRE LAYER: implement a state-space/Kalman or particle-filter model (lap_time = f(fuel) + latent_degradation, pit = state reset) that updates each lap and emits CALIBRATED 90% credible intervals, not point estimates - explicitly beating/matching ARIMA 1.520 s RMSPE. This is the single highest-signal, defensible component. (3) SURROGATE SPEED-UP: train a neural net or GP surrogate on the Monte Carlo sim so the FULL strategy space (every pit-lap x compound x stop-count, with finishing-position probability) is evaluated in <1 second, enabling true interactive what-if on the pit wall - frame this as the answer to 'safety car just dropped, decide in seconds'. (4) ROBUST + EXPLAINABLE RECOMMENDER: optimise not the expected case but a risk-adjusted objective (e.g. CVaR / maximise P(finish ahead of rival)) across a distribution of safety-car scenarios using 'ghost-car' SC modelling; output a single recommendation PLUS a strategist-readable reason (feature importance), a counterfactual ('if no SC by lap 30, switch to 1-stop'), and a confidence band. GOTCHAS to call out (shows maturity): pit-loss and SC probability are track-specific and must be parameterised per circuit; tyre 'cliff' is non-linear so linear deg models break late-stint; thin margins (literature shows tenths of a position) mean uncertainty quantification matters more than a better point estimate; public data is a proxy - architect every component so swapping in proprietary sensor telemetry only improves it. POSITIONING: do NOT claim AWS powers team strategy (it powers FOM broadcast/IT); do explicitly mirror the job's words 'real-time', 'explainable AI', 'optimisation', 'data fusion'; ship it in PyTorch/Scikit-learn with clean docs to match both the stack and the Atlassian-era 'productionise off spreadsheets' culture. THE ONE-LINE SHOCK: 'a self-calibrating, uncertainty-aware strategy engine that turns a multi-second Monte Carlo batch into a sub-second, explainable what-if you can run live on the pit wall - and here are the calibration numbers proving it.'

synthesis.modelling_spec:
CONSOLIDATED BUILD BIBLE — F1 RACE-STRATEGY ENGINE (ground-effect era 2022-2024, lap-discretized, Heilmeier/TUM backbone).

=== 0. CORE PHILOSOPHY ===
Lap-discretized (1 timestep = 1 lap). Cumulative race time per car. Three layers: (L1) deterministic+stochastic Monte-Carlo simulator, (L2) exhaustive/DP optimizer, (L3) PyTorch surrogate + Kalman live tyre updater. All circuit-specific constants are PLACEHOLDER DEFAULTS to be re-fit from FastF1 per event (see open_risks / data_playbook).

=== 1. LAP-TIME MASTER EQUATION ===
t_lap(d, L) = t_base(d) + k_fuel * m_fuel(L) + t_tyre(compound, age) + t_situational(d, L) + eps
where
  t_base(d) = t_q(track) + t_gap_racepace(track) + t_car_driver(d)
      DEFAULTS: t_gap_racepace ≈ 4.0 s above pole (TUM Spielberg 4.036). t_q is the track pole reference. t_car_driver = per-driver/car delta in s (0 reference car), CALIBRATE.
  FUEL: m_fuel(L) = m_fuel_start - b_fuel * L ; clamp >= 0.
      m_fuel_start = 110 kg (default; 105 in 2017 configs). b_fuel = total_fuel/n_laps, clamp >= 1.6 kg/lap (TUM range 1.549-2.0).
      k_fuel = 0.030 s/kg DEFAULT (track range 0.019 short low-fuel-sens e.g. Spielberg, to 0.036 long e.g. Yas Marina). => full 110 kg tank ≈ 3.3 s/lap at start, decaying linearly to 0. RECONCILIATION: ignore the 0.107 s/kg figure from arXiv:2512.00640 PDF-summary — it is ~3x the well-established value and a likely extraction error; use 0.03.
  TYRE: t_tyre = k_0(compound) + k_1(compound)*age + k_2(compound)*age^2  (QUADRATIC default — captures gentle deg + cliff onset).
      Linear (k_0 + k_1*age) = sparse-data fallback. Logarithmic (k_0 + k_1_ln*ln(k_2_ln*age+1)) = use only with rich FP long-run data (Heilmeier 2020a found it best for warm-up curvature). DO NOT use the repo's cubic form — known bug reusing quadratic coefficients.
      DEFAULT compound coefficients (s/lap; ground-effect era, CALIBRATE per event):
        k_0 (fresh offset rel. medium=0): SOFT -0.5, MEDIUM 0.0, HARD +0.5  (adjacent step ~0.5 s/lap, Austria-2025 state-space; FIA target deltas of M-H 1.2 / S-H 2.2 are NOT realised in practice — use ~0.5/~1.0).
        k_1 (linear slope): HARD 0.010-0.030 (use 0.020), MEDIUM 0.017-0.045 (use 0.030), SOFT 0.023-0.090 (use 0.060). Softest cliff compounds up to 0.18.
        k_2 (quadratic): 0.0001-0.0007 s/lap^2 default 0.0003; raise for soft/overheating-prone tracks to model cliff.
      WARM-UP: add one-off cold-tyre penalty t_cold = +1.0 s on the out-lap (age==0). Optionally let first 1-3 laps have reduced/negative effective deg (state-space found nu starts negative as tyre warms).
      GRAINING/THERMAL: NOT separate terms in v1 — absorb into per-event, per-compound k_1/k_2 fits from FP2 long-runs; flag overheating-prone tracks with steeper slope + earlier cliff.
  NOISE: eps ~ N(0, sigma_lap^2), sigma_lap driver-specific 0.46-0.86 s (default 0.6 s). For driver-mistake outliers, optionally use skewed-t error (state-space paper) instead of Gaussian.

=== 2. PIT LOSS ===
On a stop lap add PIT_LOSS[track] = in-lap loss + standstill + out-lap loss (delta vs staying out).
  Split: standstill STATIONARY ~ N(mean 2.4, tail to 3.5 s); occasional botch +4 s; world record 1.80 s. In-lap ~2.7 s, out-lap ~11.4 s (Spielberg). Stationary is only ~10% of total — do not let pit-crew speed dominate.
  DEFAULT per-track total green PIT_LOSS (s): Monaco 20, Barcelona 22, Silverstone 23, Bahrain 23, Monza 24, Singapore 28, Imola 28; GLOBAL DEFAULT 22. Range 18-30. Driven by pit-lane length & speed limit (80 km/h std, 60 km/h Monaco/Singapore).
  FIA RULE: >=2 distinct dry compounds must be used in a dry race — enforce in enumerator.
  DOUBLE-STACK: 2nd same-lap car gets queue penalty = first car stationary time ≈ +2.5 s (compounds if 1st stop slow). Want ~4-6 s gap on pit entry.

=== 3. STOCHASTIC SC/VSC MODEL (Heilmeier/TUM 2014-2019 fit) ===
RECOMMENDED (categorical):
  (a) #SC phases ~ categorical [P0,P1,P2,P3] = [0.455, 0.413, 0.099, 0.033] => P(>=1 SC)=0.545, E=0.71. SCALE to circuit P(>=1 SC): Singapore ~1.0, Baku ~0.86, Monaco ~0.25-0.29, Monza ~0.27, Paul Ricard ~0.10.
  (b) Each SC start lap ~ empirical weights over [lap1, <20%, <40%, <60%, <80%, <100%] = [0.364, 0.136, 0.136, 0.080, 0.193, 0.091] (lap-1 spike + late bump — a flat hazard underweights both).
  (c) SC duration (laps 1-10) ~ [0,0.182,0.25,0.227,0.193,0.057,0.068,0.023,0,0], mean ~4, mode 2-3.
  (d) VSC: per modelled driver retirement-by-failure trigger VSC with p=0.227; team failure prob/race 0.041-0.225. VSC duration (laps 1-4) ~ [0.479,0.396,0.021,0.104], mean ~1.75.
SIMPLER ALTERNATIVE: constant per-lap hazard lambda with 1-exp(-lambda*N_laps)=historical P(>=1 SC); each arrival SC (~0.55) or VSC (~0.45).
LAP-TIME under neutralisation: multiply green t_lap by mult_t_lap_sc=1.6 (SC) / mult_t_lap_fcy=1.4 (VSC). Optional 1-lap forming phase at 1.2x.
DEG & FUEL accrue fractionally: tyre deg *0.25 (SC) / *0.5 (VSC); fuel use *0.25 / *0.5.
GHOST-CAR: run a virtual SC-paced car; clamp real cars to it during SC laps to bunch the field (closes gaps — big positional swings) — distinguish from VSC which PRESERVES gaps.
CHEAP STOP: effective pit loss under SC ≈ green*(1-0.50) (range 40-60%), under VSC ≈ green*(1-0.35) (30-40%); absolute saving ~7-12 s (22 s -> ~10-14 s). Implement loss_eff = green_loss*(1-saving_frac), or per-track in/out deltas if available. Caveat: VSC can end with ~10-15 s warning — perfect-info sim overvalues VSC stops.
NOTE: verify against the official erratum to Heilmeier 2020 (Appl. Sci. 10, 5745) before locking these numbers.

=== 4. OVERTAKING SUBMODEL (lap-by-lap on cumulative time, TUM) ===
Per lap: sort by cumulative time; for each adjacent pair, trailing car passes iff time_advantage >= t_gap_overtake[track] - t_gap_overtake_vel*(top_speed_delta).
  t_gap_overtake (s/lap advantage REQUIRED, 2019 .ini): EASY Suzuka 1.26, Silverstone 1.35, Bahrain 1.38, Shanghai 1.50; MID Monza 1.755, Spa 1.83, COTA 1.83, Spielberg 2.01, Yas Marina 2.07, Catalunya 2.31, Budapest 2.415, Melbourne 2.70; HARD (≈unpassable) Monaco 3.75, Singapore 3.75, Montreal 3.75.
  velocity modifier ≈ -0.03 to -0.06 s per km/h top-speed delta (bigger straightline advantage lowers threshold). Equivalent team rule of thumb: need ~1 s/lap faster even WITH DRS (~0.8 s/lap clean-air).
  STOCHASTIC option (Sulsters): even when threshold cleared, pass succeeds with p_overtaking per circuit 0.10 (Mexico) - 0.40 (USA); harder tracks lower p.
DRS: bonus t_drs (negative, -0.4 to -0.5 s/lap default; TUM range -0.13 Montreal to -0.92 Singapore) applied when gap<=1.0 s at lap start, only from lap 3 (drs_allow_lap=3), disabled 2 laps after SC (drs_sc_delay=2).
TRACK POSITION emerges from MIN-GAP CLAMP: a faster car below threshold is held at min_t_dist=0.5 s (0.8 s under SC) behind and its lap time inflated to sit there, bleeding its surplus pace each lap. Add duel penalty t_duel=0.3 s/lap to both cars when fighting, and t_overtake_loser=0.3 s to the passed car the lap a pass completes (guards re-pass oscillation loops — keep >=0.3 or infinite swaps occur).
DIRTY AIR (2022+): cheapest = f1metrics tyre-wear multiplier x1.1 while within ~1 s (cost paid in deg). More physical (multi-agent TUM): linear-in-gap delta active 0.2-1.5 s, SIGN per circuit — LOSS at high-downforce (Bahrain/Monaco), small slipstream GAIN at low-downforce (Monza). Ground-effect following loss regressed from ~5%@20m / ~18%@10m (2022 launch) back toward ~20%@20m / ~35%@10m by 2025 — treat magnitude as a tunable calibrated to historical overtake counts (public data is downforce-%, not s/lap).

=== 5. MONTE-CARLO + OPTIMIZATION ===
L2 OPTIMIZER:
  (a) Deterministic free-track baseline (racesim_basic): for n_stops in [1..3]: enumerate compound sequences via itertools.combinations_with_replacement(compounds, n_stops+1) (order-independent for free-track total time; use product if order matters); enforce FIA >=2-compound + mandated start compound; place stop laps by integer search or convex/quadratic solve (deg is convex => unique optimum). Tens-to-low-hundreds of candidates => milliseconds.
  (b) Exact/competitive: DP over state=(lap, compound, tyre_age), backward Bellman minimising remaining time. Upgrade to Aguad-Thraves zero-sum feedback Stackelberg DP (leader chooses stay/pit+compound, follower responds each lap; both pick start compound pre-race) — solves hundreds of millions of states, +15% win prob vs non-strategic; yellow flags favour the trailing car.
L3 ROBUSTNESS: for EACH candidate strategy run ~10,000 stochastic races sampling SC/VSC (Sec 3), failures, lap noise (sigma 0.46-0.86), Fisk/log-logistic pit durations (Mercedes shape/loc/scale 1.563,-0.046,0.48). DO NOT pick deterministic time-optimum — score by OUTCOME DISTRIBUTION: E[finishing position], P(win/podium), and a tail measure (CVaR / 90th-pct worst). Choose on the risk-appetite efficient frontier (win-maximising is deliberately higher-variance than gap-minimising). 10,000 runs is the converged standard.
REAL-TIME PIT WALL: on SC declaration re-run candidate-strategy MC FROM CURRENT STATE (current lap, tyre age, gaps) with SC pit-loss (~10 s) + SC lap multiplier active, re-rank. For the sub-second undercut/overcut call, fall back to a 1-2 lap delta-time lookup: fresh-tyre out-lap delta (out-lap bonus ~1.0-1.5 s once warmed, steady ~1.0 s/lap fresh-vs-old) vs rival old-tyre in-lap delta. Undercut needs to be within ~1-2 s of rival, resolves over 2-3 laps; overcut wins when deg low or warm-up penalty high (gate on per-circuit passing difficulty).

=== 6. SURROGATE (L3a) ===
PyTorch MLP emulating the MC sim. Offline: sample X = {pit lap(s), start compound, stint compounds, start fuel, track state, gaps to rivals, SC prob, lap index, tyre age}; labels Y = {predicted lap time OR finishing position/Delta OR outcome mean+variance}. Arch: 3-5 hidden layers (256-128-64), ReLU, dropout ~0.2, Adam lr~5e-4, normalize inputs. Preserve stochasticity by EITHER (i) heteroscedastic Gaussian NLL predicting mean+log-variance, OR (ii) 5-MLP ensemble (spread = uncertainty). Inference ~ms => score thousands of pit-lap x compound x stop-count permutations per decision (target full strategy space in <1 s — the headline "shock"; state-space tyre models alone take 15-30 s/run). MULTI-FIDELITY: wrap a cheap analytical lap model as low-fidelity; fuse via Kennedy-O'Hagan AR1 f_H(x)=rho*f_L(x)+delta(x) (Emukit linear/NARGP) or just feed LF prediction as an extra MLP input — cuts required HF MC runs ~10x. Prefer MLP/XGBoost over GP for the main surrogate (GP O(n^3), weaker on accuracy+speed); reserve GP/co-kriging for the fusion layer where few-HF-points uncertainty matters.

=== 7. LIVE BAYESIAN TYRE UPDATER (L3b) — highest-signal component ===
Recursive Bayesian linear regression = Kalman filter. Per stint model corrected lap time = a + b*tyre_age, where corrected = raw_lap - fuel_effect (subtract k_fuel*remaining_fuel first, burn ~1.6 kg/lap). State z=[a (fresh-tyre pace), b (deg rate s/lap)]; F=I, H_t=[1, tyre_age_t], R=sigma_lap^2 (~0.1-0.3 s^2), Q=small diagonal>0 so the deg estimate ADAPTS as track rubbers-in / temp shifts (Q controls forgetting). Exact O(m^2) Gaussian posterior every completed lap => live [a,b] mean+covariance; extrapolate to forecast remaining-stint pace and optimal pit lap with CALIBRATED 90% credible intervals (target ~+/-0.15 s/lap; published deg ~0.054 s/lap). At a pit stop RESET state (re-inflate covariance / fresh-compound prior). Benchmark to beat: state-space skewed-t RMSPE 1.082 s vs ARIMA(2,1,2) 1.520 s, CRPS 0.202 vs 0.324 over 3 stints. UPGRADE to particle filter (few hundred-to-thousand particles, still real-time) only if adding compound-specific behaviour, SC regime-switching, or skewed-t errors (Kalman can't do non-Gaussian/multimodal). NOTE arXiv:2512.00640 itself uses batch HMC/Stan — the recursive filter is your adaptation; re-derive all constants from FastF1, do not copy its 0.107 s/kg.
